title: Israel Launches Major Ethnic Cleansing Escalation in West Bank, Targeting Hebron
content:
The operation follows a Palestinian resistance attack on an illegal West Bank military checkpoint.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Israeli forces on Friday began demolishing homes and businesses and forcibly evacuating residents near Hebron in the illegally occupied West Bank following a Palestinian resistance attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.

“First, we will destroy this place and completely transform it, but we will do something that has never been done before,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the scene of the shooting attack that took place earlier Friday near Hebron Junction. “We will evacuate the residents, go from house to house, remove weapons from there as well, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure.”

“We will consider expanding this model to other cities as well,” Netanyahu added.

As expected, Israel kills Palestinians every day for months on end and nobody bats an eye; Palestinians finally respond, attacking Israeli soldiers at an Israeli military checkpoint on occupied Palestinian land, and its front page news and Israel makes the entire West Bank pay. https://t.co/iaSYIE7AML

The prime minister also ordered the Israeli military to “immediately impose a lockdown on Hebron and prepare for a full lockdown” of the entire West Bank, while vowing to launch the largest military operation in the occupied territory since it was conquered during the 1967 Six-Day War and subsequently ethnically cleansed of more than 100,000 Palestinians.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz also vowed that neighborhoods associated with the attackers would be “evacuated” — a word that critics call a euphemism for ethnic cleansing — “just like in Gaza; just like in Lebanon.”

Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich echoed those calls.

“There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons, and eliminate terrorists,” he said, referring to Israel’s name for the West Bank.

“Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon,” Smotrich added.

Israeli occupation forces are forcibly evacuating residents from their homes in preparation for demolishing them in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron. pic.twitter.com/KaDpsbVFNc

Israeli forces have killed or wounded more than 250,000 people in Gaza since the Hamas-led attack of October 2023, while forcibly displacing around 1.9 million residents and destroying or damaging more than 80% of the strip’s structures. In Lebanon, nearly 40,000 people have been killed or injured by Israeli attacks over the same period, during which there were two waves of mass displacement in which more than a million people were forced from their homes each time. Dozens of Lebanese villages have been flattened.

Demolition and displacement were the order of the day in the West Bank Friday as Israeli bulldozers began demolishing homes after Netanyahu’s announcement, even as local residents said their properties had no connection to the attack on the slain Israeli troops.

The Times of Israel reported that soldiers ordered Palestinians in the Farsh al-Hawa area to evacuate ahead of demolitions, with footage showing residents being pushed out as their belongings were loaded onto trucks.

“We are already here with the equipment on the ground, sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: If you mess with us, we will exact a very, very painful price from you,” Smotrich said in Farsh al-Hawa.

Israeli occupation forces begin a large-scale demolition operation near the site of a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers and injured others in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron. pic.twitter.com/H5DEHvMKbr

Israel’s High Court intervened and issued a temporary order to halt demolitions after Arab-Israeli human rights lawyer Mohammed Dahleh filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners who claimed the destruction violated Israeli law as well as international prohibitions on collective punishment.

“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of the West Bank,” Dahleh told The Guardian. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”

Another Israeli human rights attorney, Michael Sfard, called Smotrich’s video announcement a “direct admission” of collective punishment.

The demolitions and forced evacuations are unfolding amid a wider Israeli campaign of home destruction, settler pogroms and other deadly violence, and displacement that Palestinian rights advocates and United Nations officials have called ethnic cleansing.

Palestinian olive harvesters, as well as international solidarity activists accompanying them, journalists covering settler attacks, and even international diplomats have come under attack by Israeli military-backed settler terrorists. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said earlier this week that between September 1 and October 12, Israeli settlers carried out 199 attacks connected to the harvest, killing one Palestinian, injuring 124, and damaging more than 2,500 trees and saplings.

According to OCHA, over 1,130 Palestinians — at least 250 of them children — have been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers in the West Bank since October 2023.

Friday’s developments came four days ahead of Israel’s elections, in which the ruling far-right coalition is trying to boost support among voters, including settler colonists pushing the government to annex the West Bank.

Netanyahu has vowed to annex all settler colonies. Smotrich has presented a plan to annex approximately 82% of the West Bank, excluding six major Palestinian cities. Ben-Gvir wants to annex the entire West Bank.

Israel’s actions on Friday drew widespread condemnation.

“Israeli leaders are publicly announcing plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes,” the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem said, while imploring “governments and international institutions to act now, using all means available under international law, to prevent the forcible displacement of Palestinian civilians, collective punishment, and extensive unlawful destruction in Hebron.”

author: Brooke Migdon
title: Ballot Measures Will Impact LGBTQ+ Rights in 7 States This Election
content:
Voters will decide how trans youth can participate in school sports, access gender-affirming health care, and more.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Voters in seven states this fall will weigh more than half a dozen ballot initiatives with direct bearings on LGBTQ+ people — disproportionately on transgender youth. They come as LGBTQ+ rights issues feature heavily in campaigns for candidates on either side of the aisle in the final stretch of November’s midterm elections, which will determine party control of Congress and several key governorships.

Nearly half of LGBTQ+-related ballot initiatives this year would restrict trans student-athletes from competing in line with their gender identity, an issue championed overwhelmingly by Republicans and by a rising share of Democrats. Others would ban certain transition-related treatments for minors — another focus of conservative candidates and President Donald Trump’s second administration.

Since 2021, more than half the nation has adopted laws barring trans students from playing on school sports teams matching their gender identity, and 27 states have banned gender-affirming care for trans youth. Nationally, the number of trans students who participate in school sports is unknown, but is believed to be relatively low: The Williams Institute estimates that just over 300,000 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States are trans, and not all of them will play sports.

In Washington state, where voters will decide this fall whether to ban trans student-athletes from teams matching their gender identity, the organization governing high school sports told The 19th that it is aware of about 10 trans middle and high schoolers who play sports out of more than 200,000 students who compete statewide.

Other ballot initiatives appearing before voters this fall include measures to change the state constitution to expand nondiscrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people; formally repeal language against same-sex marriages and modify students’ and parents’ rights in schools.

Here’s where LGBTQ+ rights are on the ballot this November.

Arizona voters will decide this fall whether trans student-athletes may continue to compete on school sports teams that align with their gender identity. A ballot initiative introduced late last year by state Rep. Selina Bliss, a Republican running for reelection, would effectively restore a 2022 state law restricting trans athletes’ participation that a federal appeals court had blocked in 2024.

Kris Mayes, Arizona’s Democratic attorney general, has declined to defend the law in court.

Bliss’ proposal would require public and qualifying private schools to designate K-12 sports teams as exclusively “male,” “female” or “coeducational” based on participating students’ “biological status at birth.” It would also bar trans students from using restrooms, locker rooms and other spaces “integral to athletic engagement” that match their gender identity.

In July, a lawsuit challenging the measure claimed it violated a requirement that Arizona ballot initiatives address only a single subject and was “misleading to the point of fraud.” A state superior court judge later ruled that the initiative could remain on the November 3 ballot.

Colorado voters will decide whether to bar trans student-athletes from competing in line with their gender identity by designating K-12 and collegiate sports teams based on students’ “biological reproductive systems.” The ballot initiative qualified for the general election after Protect Kids Colorado, the organization behind it, collected more than 168,000 signatures statewide.

Voters will also decide whether to ban transition-related surgeries for minors, and whether state or federal funds, Medicaid reimbursements or insurance coverage can be used to help pay for them. Such surgeries are already rare. The measure, also introduced by Protect Kids Colorado, does not directly mention nonsurgical care.

State medical organizations, including the Colorado Academy of Family Physicians and the Colorado Medical Society (CMS), the state’s largest organized group of practitioners, have publicly opposed the healthcare-related initiative. “CMS members hold diverse political views but share a core principle: medical decisions belong in the exam room,” Brigitta Robinson, the organization’s president, said in September.

That initiative also runs counter to “shield laws” safeguarding access to gender-affirming healthcare, as well as abortion, in Colorado.

In Missouri, voters will decide whether to reverse a 2024 amendment adding abortion protections to the state constitution. The new proposal would ban abortions in almost all cases, with exceptions for rape and incest, though only through the first trimester, and in medical emergencies throughout pregnancy.

It would also add language to the state constitution banning gender-affirming medical care for trans minors — prohibited by law in Missouri since 2023. An ultimately unsuccessful effort to disqualify the proposal from the November ballot, led by the ACLU of Missouri, claimed the measure violated the state’s single subject clause for ballot initiatives and failed to adequately inform voters of its intent.

Voters in Nebraska will decide whether to add language to the state constitution requiring public and qualifying private schools to designate athletic teams based on “biological sex,” and expressly declare that girls’ sports “shall not be open to students of the male sex.”

The ballot initiative qualified for the general election in August, after organizers collected more than 130,000 signatures from across the state. The following month, Nebraska voter Cara Ulman filed a lawsuit to disqualify the measure. Her legal team argued before the state Supreme Court in September that the measure’s sponsors had failed to “adequately inform the public of what they are trying to accomplish” with the initiative.

Because Nebraska’s secretary of state has already certified its general election ballot, the measure will go before voters regardless of the court’s decision, which is expected by October 27. But a ruling in Ulman’s favor would invalidate the results.

Nebraska law already prohibits trans student-athletes from participating in sports in line with their gender identity from kindergarten through college.

Voters in Vermont will decide this fall whether to add an equal rights amendment to the state constitution. The proposal, introduced in 2023 by a coalition of Democratic state lawmakers, would prohibit unequal treatment “on account of a person’s race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin.” In Vermont, a constitutional amendment must pass two legislative sessions before it can go before voters.

Virginia voters will decide whether to repeal language in the state constitution barring same-sex couples from marrying, and instead establish an affirmative right to marriage between two consenting adults regardless of their sex, gender or race. The proposal, first introduced in 2024, qualified for the November ballot after several failed attempts. In Virginia, proposed amendments to the constitution must be approved by the state House and Senate twice before they can appear before voters.

Virginia’s ban on gay marriage, added to its constitution in 2006, has been unenforceable since 2015, when the Supreme Court established a federal right to marry for same-sex couples in the United States. But marriage equality advocates have argued that recent decisions and public statements by the high court’s conservative supermajority have put that right in jeopardy. The Supreme Court declined to take up a case challenging its same-sex marriage ruling last fall.

Voters in Washington will decide whether to bar trans student-athletes from girls’ school sports teams by requiring every girl in the state to have her sex assigned at birth verified by a doctor — through either genetic or hormone tests or an examination of her reproductive anatomy — to determine eligibility for K-12 sports.

Opponents of the initiative have said it can be easily exploited, putting both trans and cisgender girls at risk of abuse. In a July op-ed, women’s soccer superstar Megan Rapinoe, a Washington native, argued the measure would drive some girls out of sports altogether.

The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has allowed trans students to compete in line with their gender identity since 2007.

The initiative qualified for the November ballot in January, after Let’s Go Washington, the political action committee behind it, collected more than 440,000 petition signatures from across the state. The group, founded by conservative hedge fund manager Brian Heywood, is also behind a second ballot measure to restore a 2024 state law regarding students’ and parents’ rights in public schools.

Washington’s Democratic-controlled legislature amended the law, known as the parental “bill of rights,” last spring, saying it was necessary to comply with existing state and federal laws. The new proposal would effectively reverse the 2025 changes.

State LGBTQ+ organizations and Democratic politicians — including Gov. Bob Ferguson — have opposed the initiative, arguing that it would put LGBTQ+ students at risk of being outed to unsupportive parents, among other safety and privacy concerns.

author: Julie Zenderoudi
title: New Study Finds EPA May Be Vastly Underreporting PFAS Levels in Drinking Water
content:
The researchers found the Environmental Protection Agency’s minimum reporting levels masked widespread contamination.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

US drinking water could contain double the PFAS levels currently reported by regulators, according to a new study from Texas Christian University.

The study, published in Cell Reports Sustainability, used computer modeling to estimate that the latest reports from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) capture only 44% of the average combined concentration of 25 polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in US water systems.

PFAS, also known as “forever chemicals,” are known to persist in the environment and are linked to some cancers, high cholesterol, reproductive issues, and other health problems.

Researchers analyzed more than 1.8 million PFAS measurement records from the EPA’s January 2026 release of monitoring data from water systems across the country. They found most individual PFAS test results in the dataset fall below the EPA’s minimum reporting levels (MRLs).

These data points are often treated as zero when agencies and researchers summarize average PFAS levels in drinking water.

The authors found that 98% of PFAS test results were below the MRL. The MRL generally means a concentration that most laboratories can reliably measure and report. However, the study’s authors argue that this doesn’t mean that the water tested is PFAS-free or that it’s safe.

“Below the reporting limit does not mean zero. Our study shows why that distinction matters when summarizing PFAS concentrations,” said lead author Gehendra Kharel, associate professor of environmental and geological sciences at Texas Christian University.

Kharel and his team used computer models applied to data from the EPA’s Fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 5), a nationwide program that requires public water systems to test drinking water for specific PFAS. They used this dataset to estimate possible concentrations for PFAS records listed below the EPA’s MRL.

They averaged hundreds of data points to come up with an estimate, performing this calculation for all 25 PFAS that had been detected at least once in the EPA’s dataset.

Under the study’s primary statistical model, they found that treating below-limit results as zero captured only 44% of the average combined concentration of the 25 PFAS monitored across 9,991 community water systems.

Jesse Goodrich, assistant professor in the division of environmental health at the University of Southern California, said that while municipal drinking water data explains why certain people have elevated chemical levels, these findings clarify why so many Americans, regardless of location or water source, have detectable PFAS in their blood.

“People traditionally have thought that drinking water is a large source of exposure to different PFAS compounds. And so when you look at the UCMR results, you see a lot of zeros, and that is hard to reconcile based on the human biomonitoring studies, where you see that everyone is actually exposed,” Goodrich said.

The results of this study are model-generated predictions rather than measurements of actual concentrations. However, Goodrich believes the results explain how trace contamination builds up.

“There’s very low levels of PFAS in drinking water, and over time, since compounds have such a long half life, that can add up to measurable, kind of ubiquitous exposure in the population,” Goodrich said.

Kharel believes the study could help provide a more complete picture of PFAS levels in US drinking water and improve how environmental monitoring data are interpreted, bridging the gap between official estimates and the actual level of chemicals in our water.

Alissa Cordner, co-director of the PFAS Project Lab at Northeastern University, said the EPA takes a more conservative approach by treating unmeasurable chemical samples as zero, which results in the lowest possible contamination estimates.

Cordner argues scientists can use better methods. Instead of assuming zero, researchers often estimate low-level presence by dividing the lab’s detection limit by either two or the square root of two.

“Either of those approaches are going to give you a less conservative and potentially more environmentally relevant measure of what’s actually going on in these samples,” she said.

Kharel recommends that agencies supplement traditional reporting methods by including estimates for below-limit results, alongside clear disclosures of detection limits, the percentage of unmeasurable samples, and margins of error.

“These practices would complement existing compliance procedures, not replace them or change health standards,” he said. Kharel and his team developed PFAS-CAST, an open-source tool designed to let agencies explore this approach with their own monitoring data.

This study comes after another report, which was published by Environment America Research & Policy Center last week, found that PFAS pollute more than 80% of tested US waterways.

In May, the EPA proposed dropping limits for four cancer-linked “forever chemicals” in drinking water established during the Biden administration, prompting concern from scientists who say even low dose exposure to PFAS can be harmful to human health over time.

“PFAS have been shown to impact human health at extremely low levels of exposure,” said Cordner. Just because standard lab tools can’t detect a chemical, “that doesn’t mean everything is zero.”

author: Jason Pramas
title: The Entire Journalism Industry Is on a Collision Course With AI
content:
News publishers either fight tech oligarchs or we lose the Fourth Estate.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

While it is not yet possible to say that the group of technologies currently called “AI” is harmful to literally everyone, that tech is already harming large numbers of people in many different ways: jeopardizing their jobs, health, privacy, and lived environment. And I can say with certainty that the way these technologies are being built, deployed, and used has been extremely harmful to the journalism industry in general and to small news outlets in particular.

It is for that reason that my organization, the Boston Institute for Nonprofit Journalism, recently joined with 59 other publishers to file a mass-action lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft. Together, this group of plaintiffs, represented by the mission-driven law firm Platkin LLP, controls more than 500 news outlets large and small across the United States.

Our main complaint is that OpenAI and Microsoft took our articles without asking our permission and definitely without providing us payment of any kind, in violation of well-established copyright law, in order to build the large-language models that are the core of their AI businesses.

This is only one type of damage that the AI giants in question have inflicted on news outlets all over the U.S. and the world. And the exposure for these companies due to that damage is absolutely huge when one combines the potential amount that our lawsuit could cost OpenAI and Microsoft with the potential amount similar lawsuits could cost those defendants — as well as the truly massive New York Times suit against the same companies on the same grounds that has been wending its way through the legal system for three years. Which, clearly, is why we are suing on those grounds.

But there are other ways the vast corporations that make up the nascent AI industry have harmed news organizations. Perhaps the worst of those is that the volume of traffic to news outlets from web search has been dropping since the AI boom began a few years ago (a dilemma that Truthout leaders have ably elucidated in two recent commentaries). We all rely upon that traffic for maintaining and, more importantly, growing our audiences over time. Audiences translate to revenue for news publications as with every other business on the web, be that revenue donations for nonprofit news groups or advertising for both nonprofit and commercial ones.

According to a January 2026 report by the University of Oxford’s Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism that used a survey “drawn from a strategic sample of 280 digital leaders from 51 countries and territories” to look at major threats faced this year by the news industry, “Aggregate data, sourced from the analytics company Chartbeat for this report, show that Google traffic from organic search to over 2,500 sites was down by a third (33%) globally between Nov 2024 and Nov 2025 and by 38% in the United States, but it is not clear how much of this is down to AI overviews.”

The news “editors, CEOs, and digital executives” surveyed for the Reuters Institute report forecast another 43 percent drop in organic search traffic to news sites this year, but we’ll have to wait until the next report to see how accurate that prediction was.

“In the past year, 170 newspapers have closed or merged, at a rate of nearly three a week, and many of these were the last remaining source of original news in their communities.”

And the fact that the study did not determine how much of that drop was due to AI search summaries does not mean that effect was insignificant. The Pew Research Center tracked 68,879 real Google searches by 900 U.S. adults in March 2025 and compared what happened when an AI search summary box (called “AI Overview” on Google) appeared on top of a search results page versus when it didn’t. The percentage that clicked through to a non-Google website link when there was no AI Overview box on top of the search results page was 15 percent. The percentage when there was an AI Overview box on top of the search results page was 8 percent. Meaning that almost half the people who would normally click through to a non-Google website link from Google search did not do so when an AI Overview box was present on top of a Google search results page.

The Pew study also found that only about 1 percent of users clicked a source link inside the AI Overview box itself. Users who saw a search summary were more likely to end their session entirely (26 percent with a summary and just 16 percent without one). So lots of people are simply reading the AI Overview on Google and then stopping their search without going to any other site, including news sites, as the Reuters Institute study showed.

Thus, a significant portion of news outlets’ audiences are being effectively blocked from finding us even as the chatbots scrape the professionally produced articles published by the news industry to answer people’s questions. This in turn strangles the reach of most news outlets and results in our audiences shrinking.

Guess what that does to our revenue streams? It’s not pretty.

All of this is happening, mind you, in an era when the news industry is already dying the death of a thousand cuts. Private equity firms and hedge funds have been buying up news outlets, mining them for profit, and selling off whatever assets were left for decades. We had already lost most of our advertising dollars to Google, our classifieds income first to Craigslist and then to other corporations, and our audiences to all the social media giants like Meta’s Facebook — which we had gamely helped bring our audiences to starting in the 2000s (“join us on Facebook!”), only to have them start to charge us to reach those same audiences not long after we helped deliver them on silver platters.

For most of the last two decades, I have been saying that the news industry is in rolling collapse, with small local and regional publications shutting down with increasing regularity.

Now I say that American journalism is in terminal collapse.

According to the 2026 State of Local News report released this month by the Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University, 7,500 newspaper jobs were lost nationwide between 2024 and 2025. This, in an industry where many reporters already don’t have full-time jobs but are forced to be freelancers and find other gigs outside journalism to make ends meet. Also, the report states, “In the past year, 170 newspapers have closed or merged, at a rate of nearly three a week, and many of these were the last remaining source of original news in their communities.”

The Medill report authors try to put a happy face on the situation by pointing out that their research shows that “8,400 news outlets make up the American local news ecosystem.” But they also demonstrate that we’ve had a net loss of 3,400 local newspapers since 2005, and that “total newspaper employment has decreased by 75% over the past two decades” (2005 to 2025).

From long experience and constant communication with dozens of fellow news publishers, I will add that I believe too many of the surviving news outlets in the U.S. are as close to shutting down as my organization — continuing to survive only by the underpaid labor of an ever-shrinking number of wildly overworked staffers shored up by a legion of “stringers” (freelancers), usually uncounted by research centers like Medill, who have little hope of ever getting a “job job” in a dying profession.

AI giants walking off with the content of news outlets like mine and blocking us from our audience with AI search summaries look to be the final nails in the coffin of the news industry as major news organizations join smaller ones in suffering significant staff cuts or going under outright.

As flawed as American journalism has always been, news publishers are beset by these manifold crises while the tech lords are amassing wealth at historic levels and using that wealth to dominate politics in ways that threaten democracy in the United States and beyond.

I believe that this crushing of remaining U.S. news outlets by oligarchs is not a bug but a feature of the tech-driven American economy. Billionaires in the tech industry (and other major industries besides) are singularly uninterested in anybody shining the light of day on their political and economic activities and those of their conglomerates.

That is why the Boston Institute for Nonprofit Journalism is committing to fighting tooth and nail to continue producing news in the service of democracy. And part of that fight is suing OpenAI and Microsoft for ripping us off — small and perennially on the brink of financial ruin though we have been throughout our entire 11+ year run to date.

We are extraordinarily pleased to be joined in this fight by many other news publishers like us, including close friends The Shoestring of western Massachusetts, ecoRI News, East Greenwich News of Rhode Island, InDepth NH, the Pelham Examiner of New York, and the Austin Chronicle of Texas.

We hope that more folks who are aware that their lives and livelihoods have been harmed by the AI giants and other tech giants will be inspired by our action and follow in our footsteps. If enough people demand redress through the legal and political system, perhaps the oligarchs will see their industries collapse before they succeed in wiping ours out — brought down by an army of regular people defending our democratic rights. On top of the deleterious effects of the growing speculative bubble forming in an AI industry unable to create products that most people are willing to pay for.

A bubble that is looking more ready to burst by the day.

author: Lauren Rankin
title: Abortion Rights Are on the Ballot in 4 States in the 2026 Midterms
content:
Voters in Missouri, Idaho, Virginia, and Nevada will decide the fate of abortion rights in their states.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Abortion is once again on the ballot. While the fate of the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House both hang in the balance, the Trump administration can still wreak havoc on abortion rights with or without congressional approval, including a backdoor ban on medication abortion. That’s why state-level measures on abortion in the 2026 midterms elections will be so consequential in the fight for reproductive rights.

This November, voters will decide the fate of abortion rights in four states. Three of those states — Idaho, Nevada, and Virginia — have initiatives that would protect abortion rights in the state. Missouri has an amendment on the ballot that undoes the results of the referendum two years ago, in which voters approved a measure to enshrine reproductive freedom in the state constitution.

Here’s a closer look at the stakes for abortion rights in each of those four states:

If you thought Missouri just did this, you’re not wrong. After Roe v. Wade was struck down in 2022, Missouri became the first state to enact a total abortion ban, without exceptions for rape or incest. But Missourians weren’t okay with that. In the 2024 general election, despite overwhelmingly going for Trump, Missouri voted to enshrine the right to abortion in the state constitution, becoming the first state to overturn an abortion ban by the direct vote of the people. That should have been the end of it — abortion was a protected right that could not be infringed by lawmakers in the state. Abortion providers and advocates began challenging the state’s restrictions in court, including an essential ban on providing medication abortion, and won.

But far right leaders like the Attorney General Catherine Hanaway and the Republicans in the Missouri state legislature have simply refused to accept defeat. Now, they’ve enjoined a near-total abortion ban (this one does contain exceptions for rape and incest, as well as fetal anomalies) with a ban on gender-affirming care for minors. Nevermind that gender-affirming care for minors is already banned in Missouri. This is a nakedly political attempt to use transphobic backlash to undo the will of the people and sneak in a ban on abortion.

If Missouri voters approve Amendment 3, nearly all abortions and gender-affirming care for minors will be banned, and a host of anti-abortion measures will also become law, including a ban on public funding for abortion and TRAP (Targeted Regulation of Abortion Providers) laws that are designed to make it more difficult for reproductive health clinics to operate.

Idaho has had a total abortion ban in effect since August of 2022, and it has had devastating consequences for the state. After its draconian abortion ban went into effect, the state lost approximately 35 percent of its practicing obstetricians, and at least three rural hospitals have shuttered their labor and delivery departments as a result. This last left Idahoans with an acute lack of access to reproductive health care, and left the remaining OBGYNs in the state overwhelmed with an increased patient load. The results are catastrophically long wait times — in Boise, it can take up to nine months to secure an appointment for an annual exam.

With Proposition 1 on their midterm ballot, Idaho voters now have a chance to reverse some of that harm. This ballot initiative would establish a fundamental right to reproductive freedom and privacy in the state. If voters approve this initiative, it would give providers and advocates an avenue to challenge the state’s total abortion ban in court and potentially legalize abortion services.

Voters in these four states will have a rare opportunity to directly vote on the status of bodily autonomy, and the results could affect us all.

While Proposition 1 is a step in the right direction, it wouldn’t carry the same weight as a constitutional amendment. Instead of codifying abortion as an inherent right in the state’s constitution, Proposition 1 would instead create a “statutory right” to abortion. Statutory rights are easier to change than constitutional rights and remain subordinate to the constitution — they can be challenged in court with a lower threshold than a constitutional amendment. If Proposition 1 passes, it would hopefully ease some of the severe restrictions facing the state, but it would be the beginning of that fight, rather than the culmination of it.

Voters in Virginia, meanwhile, have the opportunity to enshrine the right to an abortion in their state’s constitution with Question 1, the Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment. Unlike Idaho, abortion is currently legal in Virginia up to 26 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy. Virginia and North Carolina remain the only two states with legal abortion past 12 weeks in the Southeast, and Virginia is the only Southeastern state with legal abortion services past the first trimester. As such, Virginia has become a critical hub for abortion seekers — from 2020 to 2025, the number of abortions performed in the state has increased by 114 percent.

If passed, this amendment likely wouldn’t change the current status of abortion access in Virginia. The provision does allow for some restrictions on abortion in the third trimester, though abortion is currently banned in the third trimester now. But it would establish the right to an abortion in the state constitution, which makes it harder to restrict the procedure overall. And it would be an important signal to the region that it’s not just enough for abortion to be legal — it must be constitutionally protected. Abortion is a fundamental right, and by enshrining it in the state constitution, Virginians would show that no matter what the federal government does, this right will remain intact within their state’s borders.

Like Virginia, abortion is currently legal in Nevada, but with Question 6, the Right to Abortion Initiative on the 2026 ballot, Nevadans have a chance to enshrine the right to an abortion in the state constitution. This effort, led by Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom, would guarantee the right to an abortion in Nevada until the point of fetal viability, or the point at which the fetus can survive outside the womb, typically considered 24 weeks. Essentially, Question 6 would codify Roe v. Wade in Nevada and make it far more difficult for abortion opponents to ban abortion before the third trimester. It would, however, leave the door open to restrictions on abortion in the third trimester, which are already incredibly rare; only 1 percent of all abortions occur after 21 weeks.

Nevada, like Virginia, has also experienced a surge in abortion seekers since the fall of Roe in 2022. In the first year after Dobbs, Nevada experienced a 33.5 percent increase in the number of abortions. As a neighboring state to Idaho, which currently has a total abortion ban in effect, Nevada has been a mini-haven in the region for abortion seekers. If Question 6 passes, it will further entrench abortion rights in the state.

So much is at stake in this year’s midterm elections. With an entrenched autocrat in the White House, a sycophantic Congress willing to do his bidding, and a Supreme Court willing to rubber stamp some of his most heinous policies, defending the constitution and our fundamental rights has never been more essential. The White House has intentionally delayed attacks on abortion until after the midterm election, assuming that they will be politically unpopular. Voters in these four states will have a rare opportunity to directly vote on the status of bodily autonomy, and the results could affect us all.

author: Bruno Malheiro
title: The Destruction of the Amazon Is Central to the Bolsonaros’ Vision for Brazil
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro may revive his father’s program to transform the Amazon into ranches, strip mines, and plantations.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Bolsonarismo wasn’t born at the ballot box. Before it became an electoral force, it had already been taking shape along the frontiers of Brazilian capitalism, through the expansion of a territorial logic that subordinated land, nature and social relations to private accumulation. That logic legitimized the destruction of common resources and delegitimized other ways of organizing life. In 2018, maps of soy production, cattle ranching and mining overlapped with the maps showing where Jair Bolsonaro won his strongest electoral results. That wasn’t a cartographic coincidence. These frontiers were tied to political and cultural circuits, ranging from agribusiness fairs to shooting clubs to religious networks, that spread an unrestricted defense of private property, the promise of prosperity and the ideology of individual entrepreneurship. As commodity production homogenized landscapes, it also homogenized behavior and social narratives, weakening people’s ties to the land, to memory and to collective life. In the end, “agro” became “pop,” taking a central place in how meaning gets produced in Brazil.

The destruction of the Amazon is the most brutal expression of this territorial logic. Felled forests, poisoned rivers, invaded territories, and people driven out or killed: none of this is a side effect of development. These are the direct results of processes that subordinate life to private accumulation and delegitimize other ways of organizing territory. These processes sustain power relations that have expanded the far right’s strength, reach and legitimacy, and the 2018 election gave it a path into the Brazilian state.

Between 2019 and 2022, these geographies scaled up to the level of state policy, turning the Amazon into a laboratory for authoritarian experimentation. Relaxed environmental regulations, weakened enforcement, attacks on territorial rights, and the legitimization of violence in defense of private property all expanded the conditions for destruction. During this period, accumulated deforestation in the Legal Amazon reached 45,612 square kilometers, according to Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research (Inpe) and its Amazon deforestation monitoring program, known as Prodes, in 2022. The Bolsonaro administration’s agricultural policy encouraged bringing more land into the market and drove land re-concentration, while Funai, Ibama and ICMBio, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs, environmental protection and biodiversity conservation agencies, were all weakened, and environmental policy became increasingly militarized. Illegal mining expanded into Indigenous territories, linked to organized crime and enabled by the state’s tolerance. The Yanomami crisis captured this policy in its starkest form: more than 20,000 illegal miners invaded Yanomami territory, worsening river contamination and spreading disease, hunger and death, all while the government looked away.

In the Amazon, this offensive brought together sectors of traditional oligarchies with new political actors tied to predatory economic interests, including illegal ones connected to organized crime. These actors converted their economic interests into electoral power under the banner of bolsonarismo. Brazil’s so called secret budget strengthened local groups and leaders, expanding the far right’s reach across the region’s interior. This consolidation also relied on political violence, attacks on the press and the intimidation of opponents, all of which restricted critical thought and made it harder for left wing forces to organize. The Amazonian experience shows how the Bolsonaro project reshaped Brazilian patrimonialism, brought private interests closer to an authoritarian agenda and narrowed the conditions under which democracy could function.

Lula won the 2022 election by a narrow margin. His government rebuilt institutions, restored public policies, rebuilt state capacity and put Amazon protection back on the federal agenda. Brazil also regained ground in multilateral diplomacy, working to defend its interests across different blocs without aligning itself with a single center of power, a significant stance in an international landscape marked by wars and geopolitical disputes. In the Amazon, deforestation fell from 9,064 square kilometers in 2023 to 5,731 square kilometers in 2025, according to Inpe and Prodes data from 2025. Environmental enforcement resumed, operations to remove illegal occupiers confronted invasions of Indigenous lands, and territorial rights returned to the public agenda. Ibama, ICMBio and Funai also went through institutional rebuilding. Destruction, in other words, was slowed.

Despite this progress in protecting the Amazon, the first round of the 2026 election made clear that bolsonarismo‘s electoral and territorial strength has persisted. In both 2018 and 2022, the areas expanding soy production, cattle ranching, mining and deforestation overlapped geographically with the areas where Jair Bolsonaro won the most votes. In the Amazon in 2022, he won in counties that together accounted for 70% of the deforested land from the previous three decades. In 2026, separate studies once again identified these same geographies of bolsonarismo. Marcela Vecchione and Rafaella Pinto linked land concentration, properties larger than 1,000 hectares, to a drop in Lula’s vote share compared with 2022, especially along soy’s expanding frontiers. Marco Antônio Faganello, meanwhile, found sharper losses for Lula in smaller municipalities, where agribusiness carries more economic weight. Together, these studies reinforce an understanding of bolsonarismo as an electoral force sustained by a territorial logic that remains active in Brazilian society.

The rebuilding of institutions and environmental protection policies under the Lula government showed that slowing the Amazon’s destruction is possible. But this progress hasn’t dissolved the territorial foundations that sustain bolsonarismo. The 2026 election puts the country at a territorial, geopolitical and climate crossroads. The possible return of a political project that made destroying the Amazon a form of governance threatens the forest and its peoples, threatens national sovereignty given the risk of subordination to the United States, and threatens the planet’s climate balance, which the Amazon helps regulate through key biogeochemical cycles.

This election is decisive in preventing bolsonarismo from tightening its grip on the Brazilian state. Recent mobilizations by students and workers, in the streets and online, have signaled a new political force, one that needs to outlast this election’s urgency and become a lasting collective force. In the Amazon and in other biomes affected by environmental destruction, peoples and communities continue confronting the territorial forces that sustain bolsonarismo. It’s in the convergence of these different forms of mobilization that resistance to the far right can grow stronger, confronting both its territorial base and the mindset that sustains it.

Bolsonarismo turned the destruction of the Amazon into a tool for exercising power and organizing the state. But Indigenous, Quilombola, peasant, riverine and extractivist struggles, in dialogue with broader movements for rights and democracy, point toward other ways of conceiving the state, politics and our relationship with the world. It’s through the territorial experience of these forms of resistance that we can do more than confront the geographies of death that sustain bolsonarismo. We can also find geographies capable of imagining other worlds, and keep open the horizons we still need to build.

author: Simón Rodríguez
title: Dominican Republic Cozies Up to Israel Amid Right Wing Surge in Latin America
content:
The government recently adopted the IHRA definition of antisemitism while escalating its ethnic cleansing of Haitians.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On August 24, the Dominican government adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, infamous for equating opposition to Israeli apartheid and Zionist colonialism with antisemitism. President Luis Abinader made the announcement in Santo Domingo, while speaking at an event organized by the U.S. Zionist organization Combat Antisemitism Movement. Subsequently, a statement from the Dominican Foreign Ministry justified the decision by invoking a supposed official policy against hate and discrimination dating back to 1938 when, according to the text, “the Dominican State was the only one to offer asylum in Sosúa to a significant number of Jewish refugees fleeing the war crimes perpetrated by the Nazi regime”.

In 1938, the racist and genocidal Trujillo dictatorship was in power. Just as the Israeli regime pushes for the redefinition of antisemitism to shield itself, in Orwellian fashion, Abinader is rewriting the past to accommodate the neo-Trujilloist present.

It is not surprising that the Dominican government, led by Abinader, would uphold the Trujilloist legacy. This is a government that has denied the significance of slavery during the Spanish colonial period that preceded the formation of the Dominican state, that does not officially commemorate the genocide against Haitians in 1937, known as the Parsley Massacre, and that denies the existence of widespread racism in the Dominican Republic while keeping more than 200,000 Dominicans of Haitian descent stateless. President Abinader boasts of following the ideas of dictator Joaquín Balaguer, one of the Trujillo era’s main ideologues. Abinader follows in Trujillo’s footsteps regarding what Dominican racists dub “the Haitian problem,” as shown by his policy of mass deportations and the construction of a border wall — an aggiornamento of the Trujillo-era political program known as the “Dominicanization of the border.”

Today’s neo-Trujilloist regime, with its apartheid policies of racial mass deportations, denationalization and statelessness, is coherent in its support of the genocidal Israeli regime and in claiming the legacy of the dictatorship. This is the true significance of the Dominican endorsement of the IHRA definition through a statement that upholds the legacy of a totalitarian regime that extorted and killed Jewish refugees.

In the context of the ongoing genocide in Gaza, the Dominican government has signed agreements with Israel on issues such as water management and has acquired Israeli weapons. By adopting the IHRA’s working definition of antisemitism, Abinader now threatens to further erode the weak democratic rights that still exist in this Caribbean country by moving in the direction of weaponizing accusations of antisemitism to criminalize solidarity with Palestine.

Abinader’s total subordination to Trump is another key driver of his support for Israel. The Dominican government has aligned itself with the pro-Trump “Shield of the Americas” regional coalition and has made its airports available for U.S. military operations in the Caribbean and against Venezuela; it has even agreed to accept deportees from third countries arriving from the U.S.

The Dominican government’s alliance with Israel is part of this broader trend, and one of the clearest indicators of the region’s shift to the right is the intensification of ties with Israeli apartheid.

Due to a combination of strong U.S. interference and the decline of center-left parties, elections over the past year have brought right-wing governments to power in Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, and Colombia. In the cases of Bolivia and Colombia, which had no diplomatic relations with Israel, these were immediately reestablished. In Chile and Honduras, where relations had been degraded by the withdrawal of ambassadors, there was a full diplomatic normalization.

The Venezuelan government’s capitulation to Trumpism, following the U.S. military attack on January 3, 2026, and the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro, is also part of this regional shift to the right. Interim president Delcy Rodríguez reestablished diplomatic relations with Israel in August, following a campaign of “disaster diplomacy” by Netanyahu, who took advantage of the twin earthquakes in northern Venezuela that left more than 6,500 dead and tens of thousands injured. Relations had been broken since 2009.

In turn, the adoption of the IHRA’s definition of antisemitism has become an indicator of how closely Latin American regimes align with the objectives of Israeli foreign policy and their willingness to criminalize solidarity with Palestine. The definition in question was drafted in 2004 and adopted by the IHRA in 2016, after which it was promoted by Israeli foreign policy as part of its “new antisemitism” doctrine, which views opposition to Israel as the most significant form of antisemitism. Its text includes questioning the democratic character of the State of Israel among its examples of antisemitism. The definition was referenced in a Trump executive order in 2019 and in Latin America it has been adopted by right-wing governments in Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama, Guatemala, and Uruguay before being adopted by the Dominican Republic.

Over the past two years in Argentina, legal proceedings have been initiated, using the IHRA definition, against Alejandro Bodart, Vanina Biasi, and Mariano Soria, leaders of the Left and Workers’ Front-Unity, a Trotskyist coalition that holds four seats in the National Congress. In Brazil, socialist leader Zé María of the PSTU and the Jewish journalist Breno Altman have been criminalized for criticizing the Israeli state and calling for Palestinian freedom “from the river to the sea.” Zé María was sentenced to two years in prison, Altman was fined, Bodart won an appeal that overturned his conviction, and the cases against Biasi and Soria remain open.

Kenneth Stern, the main drafter of the IHRA definition, who describes himself as a liberal Zionist, has criticized its use by right-wing Jewish sectors to limit freedom of expression and foster a McCarthyist environment, citing the case of Germany, where authorities have used it to label Jewish people as “anti-Semites” for opposing Israeli crimes in Gaza. Stern recommended the U.S. Senate in 2025 to not adopt the IHRA definition.

Dominican legal scholar Jaime Rodríguez has pointed out that, within the Dominican legislative framework, the Abinader administration’s endorsement of the IHRA definition is not yet legally binding, though he has warned of the risks of censorship and persecution that would result from moving forward with enshrining it into law. Democratic guarantees and freedoms in the country are already fragile, and the alliance with Israel has contributed to their weakening, as evidenced by the Dominican government’s use of the Israeli spyware Pegasus against journalists.

But the peril is an even greater one. There is a clear affinity between the Neo-Trujillista regime led by Abinader and the Zionist project, as Israel is viewed by the Dominican right as a blueprint for Dominican apartheid. Neonazi organizations regularly wield Israeli flags at racist marches against Haitians. Much like Trujillo in 1938, Abinader is unconcerned about antisemitism or discrimination more broadly, as the regime he leads is carrying out a brutal crackdown on Haitian migrants and Dominicans of Haitian descent, conducting a campaign of more than one million deportations over the past six years during which dozens of people have been killed and many more subjected to horrific violence. Normalizing genocide abroad is a way of normalizing apartheid and ethnic cleansing it at home.

author: Shahad Ali
title: Netanyahu May Lose Israeli Elections. That Won’t Save Gaza From Occupation.
content:
As living conditions here in Gaza deteriorate, we have little hope that Israel’s elections will ease our suffering.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Israel is scheduled to hold general elections on October 27, with a fierce contest between incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party. These will be the first elections since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel.

The continuation of suffering in Gaza has been exploited as a political tool to attract more votes in Israel’s electoral struggle. The Likud party, led by Netanyahu, has cited ongoing military operations and the assassinations of Palestinian faction leaders in Gaza as evidence that its military strategy is working, warning that its opponents would end the war without fully destroying Hamas. It also frames the election as a decisive battle to protect Israel from the establishment of a Palestinian state and prevent the Palestinian Authority from returning to govern Gaza. The party argues that an opposition victory would mean yielding to international pressure and accepting a two-state solution.

Likud’s campaign rhetoric has unfolded alongside calls from its far right coalition partners for the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians from Gaza and the re-establishment of Israeli settlements in the Strip. Both Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister and leader of the Religious Zionism party, and Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister and leader of the Jewish Power party, have championed rebuilding Israeli settlements in Gaza since October 7, 2023, framing the war as an opportunity to reverse the 2005 disengagement. Moreover, as part of his election campaign, Ben-Gvir has proposed a seven-year plan, which he calls “Disengagement 710,” to relocate approximately 1.86 million Palestinians from Gaza.

On the other hand, Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Netanyahu and leader of Israel’s Yashar party, pledged to remove Hamas from power in Gaza and destroy its military wing within 18 months of becoming prime minister. Speaking near the Gaza border, he said he would work to end Hamas’s rule in the Strip, either by implementing U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan, which Netanyahu’s government had approved, or through military force.

In Gaza, most people see no real difference between Benjamin Netanyahu and rivals such as Gadi Eisenkot. In our view, Gaza’s future will not be determined at the Israeli ballot box. Both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s parties and members of their coalition are likely to pursue similar policies toward our cause. Although the leading parties may have different ideas and methods, their policies ultimately serve the same goal: destroying Gaza and reshaping its reality and culture to give it an Israeli character.

As the election approaches, humanitarian conditions in Gaza continue to deteriorate. Israeli forces are intensifying their military operations across the Strip through airstrikes, artillery fire, and the expansion of the area under their control, known as the Yellow Line. Since the ceasefire agreement was announced on October 10, 2025, ongoing Israeli attacks have killed 1,522 Palestinians and injured 5,421 others. Israeli forces now control an estimated 63 percent to 70 percent of the Strip and continue to seize additional land. Recently reported expansion into more areas of eastern Gaza City has forced many families to flee without a suitable place to go.

The International Organization for Migration warns that approximately 1.8 million people in Gaza face a fourth winter without adequate protection from rain, flooding, and cold. Meanwhile, Israeli authorities continue to block the entry of emergency shelter supplies, timber for repairs, heating equipment, and winter clothing through the crossings.

In addition to this, the Israeli Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) announced in a statement on October 15 that coordination for the entry of commercial goods into Gaza had been suspended. COGAT claimed that the decision was made by local merchants in Gaza, who had grown frustrated with Hamas’s imposition of taxes on their trucks. However, Jihad Esleem, deputy head of the Private Transport Association in Gaza, announced on October 19 that an official agreement had been reached with the Israeli side to resume operations at the Kerem Shalom crossing, allowing truck movements to resume and commercial goods to enter the Gaza Strip.

Although the closure of the crossing did not last long, it heightened Gazans’ concerns that such closures could happen again at any moment, with Hamas used as a pretext. The closure led to shortages of food and other basic necessities, including clothing and essential shelter materials, as well as significant price increases.

The price of a 25-kilogram bag of flour has risen from 70 shekels to 150 shekels, putting it beyond the reach of many families in Gaza.

Humanitarian aid alone cannot meet the needs of the entire population. Commercial goods must also be allowed into Gaza to ensure that essential supplies are available at affordable prices. We are already beginning to see the effects of the closure. Take flour, for example: the price of a 25-kilogram bag of flour has risen from 70 shekels to 150 shekels, putting it beyond the reach of many families in Gaza, where the war has caused widespread poverty and unemployment. Moreover, vegetables, fruits, eggs, and chicken have become increasingly scarce because Israel continues to restrict their entry, even after resuming commercial operations through the Kerem Shalom crossing.

Beyond these immediate concerns, what we fear most is that the upcoming Israeli elections could trigger a resumption of the war. Netanyahu might use a renewed war to postpone the vote and salvage his political future, especially as polls have suggested the possibility of his electoral defeat. According to Haaretz military analyst Amos Harel, Netanyahu views losing the election as a serious personal threat. Harel added that people who have spoken with Netanyahu in recent years believe he is convinced that electoral defeat would lead to his conviction in his criminal trial.

Ranya Hammouda, a 45-year-old mother of five children in Gaza whom I met while she was trying to light a fire to cook for her children, told me she had no hope that her family’s conditions would improve if the Israeli government changed. She told me:

The Board of Peace plan for Gaza will remain ink on paper, as I do not believe that either Netanyahu or Eisenkot will move forward with it. From the beginning, I saw this plan as an illusion that we desperately clung to in the hope that our suffering might end one day and we could return to our normal lives.

We will continue to live under the same harsh conditions in flimsy tents, deprived of the most basic human dignity and struggling to obtain even food and water. I believe that the suffering we endured last winter will be repeated this winter. Our tent is now torn after two years of use, and I fear that strong winds and rain will cause it to collapse. On top of that, we do not have enough winter clothes or blankets. My only wish now is that winter would not come at all, because I know the suffering that awaits us … I fear that we might pay with our blood for the promises Benjamin Netanyahu makes to appease extremists. I fear that he might order vicious attacks against us simply to win more votes and bolster his election campaign.

Mohamed Abu Raylah, a 29-year-old programmer who is currently living in what remains of his home in Al-Shati Camp also told me that he no longer follows the Israeli elections or hopes that Netanyahu’s defeat might ease Palestinians’ suffering. He said he believes all the leading Israeli parties are the same, differing only in name:

The policies of killing, displacement, and destruction, passed down through Israeli generations since 1948, will continue until they achieve their goal of taking control of all Palestinian land and expelling its inhabitants…. Whether Netanyahu leaves and Eisenkot takes his place, each will use an escalation of military operations in Gaza to convince the Israeli public that he is building on past achievements rather than destroying them. The same scenario will continue: siege, suffocation, and war. Their mentality will not change. It is the mentality of an occupying power that believes we must be wiped out.

For Abu Raylah and many others in Gaza, the rivalry between Israeli politicians means nothing when Palestinians continue to be denied their rights and freedom regardless of who holds power in Israel.

“None of them will come along and give us our rights,” Raylah concluded. “Change won’t come from them. It will come from our own steadfastness.”

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Courts Reject Trump’s Attempt at Deploying ICE to Intimidate Voters
content:
A judge ordered Homeland Security to stop sending agents door to door in nine key states to hunt for “voter fraud.”

A judge ordered Homeland Security to stop sending agents door to door in nine key states to hunt for “voter fraud.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Trump administration is attempting to intimidate Latino voters and naturalized citizens with the threat of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids and arrests ahead of the midterm elections, democracy advocates are warning.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has deployed federal agents in multiple states to knock on doors and demand voters verify their identities and registration as part of an “Unlawful Voter Initiative” launched in August. In response to a lawsuit filed on October 19 by labor and voting rights groups, a federal judge in California ruled the DHS initiative violates the Voting Rights Act and ordered federal agents to halt “elections-related field operations and field interviews” in California, Wisconsin, New York, Missouri, Connecticut, Nevada, Georgia, Pennsylvania, and Washington.

“I look at this list of states, and I can think of some high-profile races that may be anticipated to be close in a lot of those jurisdictions,” said David Janovsky, senior policy analyst and acting director of the Constitution Project at the Project On Government Oversight, in an interview. “So, I think there is a reasonable question in all of this about how the federal government is choosing to focus these efforts, and the motivation that is behind that.”

Critical contests in these states include the tight race between Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia, which could decide which party has a majority in the Senate. In California, New York, and beyond, multiple races could help to determine control of the House or pad a Democratic majority.

Janovsky said sending agents door-to-door in states where Republicans face headwinds could suppress turnout. Indeed, since the 2024 election, polls suggest that Latinos and many other voters turned against the GOP as ICE invaded major cities such as Chicago and Minneapolis, causing chaos, fear, and death.

By deploying federal immigration agents to go door-to-door hunting for so-called “voter fraud” ahead of Election Day, the Trump administration may also be preparing the ground for meddling with election results and suppressing dissent if Republicans perform poorly and lose their congressional majority.

With billions of dollars in funding from Congress, the Trump administration has transformed ICE into a powerful tool of intimidation. ICE agents have injured and killed people in multiple high-profile cases since Donald Trump took office again. Under Trump’s mass deportation campaign, ICE has detained at least 506 U.S. citizens as well as many legal permanent residents. People arrested by ICE are often jailed in facilities where dozens have died amid complaints of medical neglect, including a lawful permanent resident who was found dead in a Texas ICE jail last week.

Trump’s Justice Department has been trying for over a year to get voter rolls from every state and hand them over to DHS investigators searching for evidence of widespread fraud that experts say does not exist. DHS uses voter data to create “target lists” of potentially fraudulent voter registrations, according to Wednesday’s court order.

“With Homeland Security agents knocking on people’s doors asking them if they are properly registered to vote, there is a very real concern, and it’s pretty well known, that the federal government doesn’t have accurate data,” Janovsky said. “It could freak people out, like, ‘maybe I don’t want to register to vote and put myself on this list.’”

Under an executive order issued in May 2025, the Department of Justice demanded voter rolls from states to share with DHS so agents could scour for non-citizens attempting to vote, which is exceedingly rare. States run elections, not the federal government, but many red states handed voter data over voluntarily. Another 26 states, including those named in Wednesday’s order, saw lawsuits filed by the Justice Department over voter rolls dismissed by federal courts.

“That effort has largely been rejected by the courts, because basically the federal government has no real business micromanaging every state’s voter rolls,” Janovsky said.

Unable to force states to hand over voter data, DHS gathered more than 48 million voter records through independent and commercial sources “of questionable provenance” in order to search for potential fraud, according to Wednesday’s ruling. DHS records obtained by Democracy Forward under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) link these efforts to Heather Honey, a prominent 2020 election denier who has supplied Trump with conspiracy theories and is currently serving as a senior advisor to DHS and ICE.

The FOIA records also reveal that the Trump administration considered sending undercover agents to investigate pro-democracy groups that register people to vote, particularly in Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

Critically, the court order halting the DHS door-knocking initiative highlights the significant likelihood that such investigations would result in errors and the misidentification of citizens as non-citizens, potentially preventing them from voting, according to Elizabeth Laird, director of equity at the Center for Democracy & Technology.

“This decision continues to establish the legal basis that it is not only unethical but illegal to weaponize personal data in ways that lead to irreparable harm to individuals who are wrongly targeted,” Laird said in a statement on Thursday.

While Laird said the initial ruling is a promising step forward, the case underscores the “significant dangers” of the Trump administration’s “ongoing efforts to compile and weaponize personal information from across federal and state agencies.”

“That is the high-level problem,” Janovsky said of the administration’s exploitation of voter data. “Then you have these targeted enforcement operations happening in a handful of states, including California.”

California may be a testing ground of sorts, Janovsky said. Immigrant advocates have confirmed a rapid increase of ICE arrests in the Central Valley and beyond, with more than 100 farmworkers arrested last week alone. As California’s KQED reports, fear and rumors spread whenever ICE conducts large enforcement operations. People stay home as a result, causing Latino businesses to suffer, schoolchildren to miss classes, and patients to forgo seeing the doctors.

Advocates warn the Trump administration is betting that ICE could keep Latino voters away from the polls as well, but Democratic California Rep. Lateefah Simon says the intimidation campaign will not work. Indeed, election officials are seeing a surge of interest in early voting, with 21 million people casting early ballots as of Friday morning, NPR reports.

“We know what Republicans are trying to do — intimidate Latino citizens so they stay at home and don’t exercise their right to vote,” said Simon in a statement to local media on October 16.

Activists are preparing for the potential deployment of ICE agents to the polls, which Trump officials have said is not a priority but also could not be ruled out. In Arizona, the grassroots LUCHA coalition has trained hundreds of volunteer “constitutional defenders” to respond to federal intimidation if it were to occur on Election Day, according to communications director César Fierros.

“Masked agents in tactical gear threatening people in line or attempting to raid polling locations would be an assault on democracy itself, and it’s the greatest threat facing our nation,” Fierros told Truthout in an email. “We are preparing, but hoping for the best.”

On Monday, the Justice Department announced it was charging 28 non-citizens in California with election crimes, a development Janovsky is watching closely. On October 15, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit against California that asks a federal court to order California officials to stop processing ballots from thousands of people the Trump administration identifies as “likely non-citizens.”

Before filing the lawsuit, federal officials delivered a flash drive to Los Angeles County that contained 20,000 names and a 48-hour deadline to investigate them for fraudulent voter registrations. When local and state officials refused to do so, citing security concerns and potentially faulty data, Trump wrote online that, “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”

The administration’s data has already proven to be faulty in the neighboring state of Nevada, where DHS officials recently claimed to have identified nearly 16,000 non-citizens registered to vote on state rolls. However, that number fell to 185 after further inquiry, and then to zero after state officials confirmed that those individuals were all U.S. citizens.

While Janovsky said the circumstances surrounding the charges of election crimes against 28 individuals are unclear, the Trump administration has consistently claimed to be fighting widespread voter fraud that does not exist — but such enforcement backs up bogus claims about fraud that Trump has made since losing the 2020 election.

“It’s entirely possible that some of these folks are citizens who were properly registered to vote and the feds have bad data — and that is the basis for the court injunction issued on Wednesday,” Janovsky said.
