author: Amy Goodman
title: At Least 59 People Have Died in ICE Custody Since Start of Trump’s Second Term
content:
Meanwhile, the GEO Group announced that DHS purchased two immigration jails in Adelanto, California, for $950 million.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

At least 59 people have died in ICE custody since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, the highest number in more than a decade. Many deaths have been linked to medical neglect, including four of five recent deaths at California’s Adelanto Processing Center, according to a 2026 report by the state attorney general. Al Jazeera English’s Fault Lines investigated deaths at the facility, which is operated by the private prison company GEO Group, in the new documentary Dying in Detention.

“GEO Group has made over a billion dollars in profits from immigration detention. They have given more than a million dollars … to help reelect Donald Trump,” says correspondent Natasha Del Toro. “That raises a lot of questions for us about the relationship between GEO and the federal government, and some of these conflicts of interest.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman in Los Angeles. Juan González is in Chicago.

We’re turning now to the rising numbers of deaths in ICE custody. At least 59 people have died in immigration detention since the start of Trump’s second term, the highest in more than a decade, and a growing number of people are dying from medical neglect. Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old legal permanent resident who died earlier this month at an ICE detention center run by the private GEO Group in Laredo, Texas, has complained to his daughter for months about the lack of medical care in detention. At the Adelanto Processing Center, just north of where I am right now in Los Angeles, four out of five recent deaths were linked to substandard medical care. That’s according to the California attorney general’s report on ICE detention centers in California this year.

Journalist Natasha Del Toro and Al Jazeera’s Fault Lines investigated the deaths at the Adelanto Processing Center, which is run, yes, again, by the private GEO Group. This is a clip from the Fault Lines episode Dying in Detention.

JESUS ORTIZ RUIZ: You gotta be literally dying here for you to get sent to the hospital.

NATASHA DEL TORO: We’re traveling to one of the deadliest immigration detention facilities in the United States. The Adelanto ICE Processing Center sits on the edge of the High Desert in California.

JESUS ORTIZ RUIZ: There’s four people in the cell with us. We’re at max capacity right now.

NATASHA DEL TORO: We’ve been speaking with people detained there, people who made it out.

[translated] What are the conditions like inside?

MELVIN: [translated] Not very good.

MELVIN’S DAUGHTER: I’ve never seen him like this.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Is it shocking to see him?

MELVIN’S DAUGHTER: He looks older.

NATASHA DEL TORO: He looks older.

And hearing from family members whose loved one went in and didn’t come out alive.

JOSE MIGUEL AYALA: I feel like they’re just treating these people like animals, in a way. None of these deaths should have happened.

NATASHA DEL TORO: As the Trump administration continues to detain record numbers of immigrants, more and more are dying behind bars.

DR. NICHOLAS CUNEO: The number of deaths has more than tripled. The risk of death in ICE detention has never been higher.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Adelanto is run by the for-profit prison company The Geo Group. Four immigrants died there in a recent six-month span. Detainees have fought for better conditions, filing a lawsuit and going on a hunger strike.

JULIUS FREDERICK: They retaliate against you. They just come in, they grab you, and they take you to solitary confinement.

ASHRAF ABUJUMA: They beat me up. I don’t know if you can see, like, bruises all over my body.

AMY GOODMAN: One of the people who died recently at the Adelanto ICE jail in California was Ismael Ayala-Uribe. This is another clip from the documentary Dying in Detention.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Ismael Ayala-Uribe died after becoming sick in an immigration detention center in California in September 2025. He was 39 years old. He was one of more than 50 people to die in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, during President Trump’s first 500 days back in office.

JOSE MIGUEL AYALA: He was very protective of, like, not just us, but my mom and dad, too.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Ismael was born in Mexico and came to the United States undocumented when he was 5. He grew up in Southern California and was later granted DACA, a program that gives some immigrants who came here as children temporary protection from deportation.

JOSE MIGUEL AYALA: He was a good uncle. He was — the kids needed something, he would always go get it, get them school clothes, supplies or whatever they needed, you know? And they do miss him.

NATASHA DEL TORO: He worked at this local car wash just outside Los Angeles for 15 years, supporting his family and eventually becoming the owner’s right-hand man. In 2015, he was convicted of driving under the influence and lost his DACA protections. That left him vulnerable to deportation when President Trump returned to the White House and ramped up immigration raids across the country.

AMY GOODMAN: For more, we’re joined now from Tampa, Florida, by the journalist Natasha Del Toro, investigative correspondent of Fault Lines from Al Jazeera English, the most recent documentary, Dying in Detention.

Watching this documentary, your heart breaks, Natasha. This story of Ismael, 39 years old, dies of an abscess in the year 2026 because an infection that was left to fester goes into his bloodstream. Tell us more about this story.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Yeah, Amy, thank you so much for giving space to this story. It’s so important, and it’s happening right here in our country.

So, as you all noted, Ismael Ayala-Uribe was 39. He came to this country when he was 4 or 5 years old. His parents brought him from Mexico. And he had DACA protections, which he lost because of a DUI. He had lost — he had worked at this car wash for 15 years, was the right-hand man to the owner, and then was picked up in these ICE raids that happened last summer, where they picked up hundreds of workers, people at their place of work, but they figured that — you know, ICE figured that they would be able to get a lot of undocumented people there. And that’s where they picked up Ismael, took him down to Adelanto.

Ismael had gotten sick pretty quickly while he was there. He started complaining of fever. He had chills, started getting very pale. And he was complaining of a sore that was, he said, 10 out of 10 pain. But initially he was ignored when he asked for medical help. Finally, it got so bad that they had to rush him to the infirmary, ended up giving him a Tylenol, which is what we heard over and over again, that they — no matter what they were complaining of, they would get a Tylenol. And they didn’t actually catch the source of the problem, because no one did an examination of the place where he was feeling pain, which was this infected abscess, which, like you said, in 2026, this is really an easy thing to catch. All you need is, you need an antibiotic, is really what you need. But because no one did an examination, no one gave him an antibiotic. He developed sepsis and went into sepsis shock, and ultimately had to go to the emergency room. Finally, they took him to the emergency room. But it’s there that that he died. And we spoke with a physician for human rights who examined — who looked through his medical reports and told us that this was a very preventable death.

Sadly, what we found is that what happened to Ismael is not an isolated incident. This is actually part of a much larger pattern.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And I wanted to ask you, Natasha — he died at 2:30 in the morning, and his family was not notified by ICE. It was the local police that notified them. What is the — how are family able to communicate with those of their family members who are detained in these centers?

NATASHA DEL TORO: Sure. They are able to go to the center. And Lucia, Ismael’s mom, who we spoke to, said she had gone there. Mind you, this is two hours away from Los Angeles. They live in Orange County. And they were driving there as often as they could. So, they were able to communicate with their loved ones by visiting the center. But as you noted, they were not — they were not notified of the death until the next morning, when Lucia and Jose, the brother, got a knock at the door and said that Ismael was dead, that he had passed.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Could I ask you also — the GEO Group announced recently that the Department of Homeland Security had purchased two immigration detention centers in Adelanto for $950 million. What’s the significance of this, of a center going from private ownership to government ownership?

NATASHA DEL TORO: Sure. And this was a very recent announcement that was made. We had actually wrapped up our reporting when we found out that the government had actually purchased the GEO Group. We are not entirely sure why they decided to purchase Adelanto, but what I can tell you is that there are several class-action — there are lawsuits against the Adelanto facility because of the conditions inside. Many of the detainees filed lawsuits. And what we believe is that it becomes harder to sue if it’s in government hands versus if it’s owned by — you know, in private hands. What we do know, though, is that Adelanto is also — it’s going to continue to be run by the GEO Group. So, even though the U.S. government has bought the facility, it’s still going to be operated by GEO.

We also found in our investigation that there were a lot of ties, a lot of conflicts of interest between the federal government and the GEO Group. For example, the director of ICE is somebody who was an executive, a high-level executive, at the GEO Group, somebody named David Venturella. Also, Jim Jordan, who we confront in the film, who is the — you know, he’s the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. It was leaked that he received, or a PAC tied to him received, a $250,000 contribution from the GEO Group. As a chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, he is supposed to provide oversight of these immigration detention centers, and yet groups tied to him are receiving substantial donations from the GEO Group.

And then, finally, you know, GEO Group has made over a billion dollars in profits from immigration detention. They have given more than a million dollars in campaign — like, to help reelect Donald Trump. So, part of his campaign donations, he received more than a million dollars. So, obviously, that raises a lot of questions for us about these — the relationship between GEO and the federal government and some of these conflicts of interest.

AMY GOODMAN: We just have 30 seconds, Natasha, but I want to ask: Is it possible the number of people who’ve died after medical care failings could be higher, given the rapid deletion of documents by the Trump administration?

NATASHA DEL TORO: Oh, yeah. I mean, we’ve had a hard time giving concrete numbers, mostly because, first, they keep increasing. I mean, someone died just the weekend, a few days ago, in Texas. But also, they recently changed their reporting requirements. So, now ICE does not have to report deaths for anybody held in custody up to 30 days after. They do not have to report those deaths. So, it’s entirely possible that there have been more, that the numbers are not current and they’re not accurate, because they are cutting the requirements, the reporting requirements. Also —

AMY GOODMAN: Natasha Del Toro —

NATASHA DEL TORO: — one more thing I want to mention —

AMY GOODMAN: — I want to thank you so much for being with us, and we’re going to link to your documentary, called Dying in Detention.

That does it for our show. Tonight at 6:30, I’ll be at Stanford University at the CEMEX Auditorium for the screening of Steal This Story,” Please!, in conjunction with the U.N. Association Film Festival. On Saturday, 6:30 at the New People Cinema in Japantown, San Francisco. Sunday at Smith Rafael Center in San Rafael. Monday and Tuesday in Boulder, Colorado, and Fort Collins. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

author: Chris Walker
title: Kagan Warns Far Right Supreme Court Rulings Will Undermine American Democracy
content:
The American people view the current political system as “a nightmare,” Kagan said, “and they’re right.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan warned a group of law students at Catholic University on Tuesday that the current iteration of the court — which has a 6-3 majority of far right conservatives — is upending American democracy.

Kagan focused much of her remarks on addressing gerrymandering over the past year by both political parties. The map-changing began when Republicans started redrawing districts in order to get an upper hand over Democrats in the midterms. Democrats responded in kind, redrawing maps in states where they were more likely to see gains to counter the Republicans’ efforts.

(Democrats have also submitted legislation to prevent these “gerrymander wars” in the future by requiring nonpartisan boards to redraw maps going forward, a proposal that Republicans have rejected.)

“Both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting equality,” Kagan lamented in her lecture to the law students.

Such gerrymandering pushes political parties “toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about anymore is being primaried,” Kagan said.

It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so. In this election, and the next election, we are seeing large states with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is very destructive to our democracy.

Through these redistricting efforts, many conservative states ended up gerrymandering Black residents out of districts where they were the majority, thus reducing their voices in Congress. The conservative-led Supreme Court upheld that process this year, ruling that enforcement mechanisms for the Voting Rights Act that preserved Black-majority districts were unconstitutional, a finding that Kagan dissented from.

She elaborated on her opposition to that opinion on Tuesday.

“I think part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions. … The court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should,” Kagan said.

The liberal justice also discussed the Supreme Court’s rulings on campaign finance, which have opened up the floodgates of influence spending by millionaires and billionaires in recent years.

“The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” Kagan said.

Polling shows that a majority of Americans are indeed upset with the current iteration of the nation’s high court.

In an Economist/YouGov survey conducted at the end of the Supreme Court’s term earlier this year, only 36 percent of voters gave the justices overall approving marks, while 50 percent voiced disapproval of the court. There was a notable partisan edge in favor of liberal bloc members of the court, the poll found, noting that every member of that bloc received net positive ratings, while every conservative justice on the court received negative ratings.

The Supreme Court’s rulings threaten to undermine election safety, too, said Dan Canon, professor at the Louis D. Brandeis School of Law, in an op-ed for Truthout earlier this week.

“What harm might result from the opinions of today’s Court, an institution unmistakably captured by a power-hungry executive? In a nation of this size, facing democratic decay this severe, there is no such thing as a safe prediction,” Canon wrote. “But if you’re the gambling type, the smart money is on a spectacularly violent future for U.S. elections, if not in the upcoming midterms, then likely by 2028.”

“At their best, independent courts channel even the most heated political grievances into nonviolent resolutions,” Canon said. “If an apex court abdicates that role by disenfranchising voters, institutionalizing clientelism, and shielding executive lawlessness, it removes the pressure valves that keep democratic competition peaceful.”

Pointing to rulings on voter exclusion, corruption, constraints on the executive branch, and more, Canon concluded that such violence may come sooner than most may think.

“If unprecedented violence does not attend the next few U.S. elections, it will be in spite of this Supreme Court, not because of it,” he said.

author: Dottie Rosenbaum
title: SNAP Participation Losses Far Exceed CBO’s Estimates
content:
About 5.5 million people lost food assistance through SNAP in the year since enactment of the 2025 reconciliation law.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

About 5.5 million people lost food assistance through SNAP in the year since enactment of the 2025 reconciliation law. This includes about 2 million children, who were not targeted by the law’s eligibility restrictions.

These participation declines have resulted in a sharp drop in SNAP spending, since 90 percent of SNAP spending is for food assistance benefits. (The rest is primarily administrative expenses and Puerto Rico’s nutrition assistance block grant.)

SNAP spending in fiscal year 2026, which ended September 30, was nearly $11 billion lower than the prior year (-10.3 percent). Along with the 5.5 million people who have less money to purchase groceries, this also means people in communities across the U.S. had about $11 billion less for spending on food in fiscal year 2026.

The drop in SNAP participation and spending is considerably more than the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) predicted. The latest U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) data for July 2026 show that monthly SNAP participation in fiscal year 2026 is on track to average about 4.5 million fewer people compared to the average month in fiscal year 2025 — far greater than CBO’s prediction of 2.8 million fewer people in an average month in 2026 versus 2025. (See chart.) CBO projected that SNAP outlays would drop by about $6 billion in 2026; in actuality SNAP outlays dropped by nearly double that amount.

The most likely reason for the larger-than-expected cut is the impact of the 2025 reconciliation law shifting enormous new SNAP costs to states, which they owe starting in fiscal year 2028. CBO estimated the cost shift mandate would have no impact until 2028. But it has already led many states to erect barriers to people’s SNAP participation, such as more paperwork and other requirements that states often don’t have the staff to administer.

The reconciliation law granted a few states a two-year delay for this harmful cost shift. Congress should extend the delay to all states before the end of the year, given SNAP losses outpacing predictions and the high cost of groceries and other basic needs. CBO estimated the reconciliation law would cut SNAP by $187 billion (about 20 percent) through 2034, the largest SNAP cut in history. With far steeper cuts evident in fiscal year 2026, Congress should not further cut SNAP to offset the cost of a delay in the cost shift.

In its most recent February 2026 baseline, CBO projected that 39.3 million people would participate in SNAP in an average month of 2026, compared to about 42.1 million in 2025. But just shy of 36.1 million people participated in SNAP in July 2026, according to the most recent data from USDA, suggesting that fiscal year 2026 participation will average about 37.6 million people, or about 4.5 million below last year’s average.

SNAP spending was also substantially lower than CBO’s forecast. CBO’s most recent baseline assumed a 6 percent drop in SNAP spending between fiscal years 2025 and 2026. But SNAP spending for the fiscal year was more than 10 percent, or nearly $11 billion, lower than it was in 2025.

The outsized drops suggest that people not ostensibly targeted by the 2025 reconciliation law’s eligibility restrictions are losing SNAP anyway. That includes many children, seniors, and people with disabilities, yet another reason for Congress to delay the cost shift.

At the time of the reconciliation law’s enactment, CBPP explained that, based on CBO’s estimate, once the law had fully taken effect about 4 million people would be cut from SNAP entirely or lose a substantial amount of their benefits. Now, with nearly a year of USDA data since the law’s enactment, more than 5.5 million fewer people receive any SNAP. That figure does not include people whose benefits are lower as a result of the new law. More losses are almost certain as the law continues to phase in.

That the losses are coming faster than CBO predicted is likely in large part because CBO’s original estimates did not factor in any effects of the state cost shift mandate until 2028. This is when the law requires states will to start paying for a share of SNAP benefits — 5 to 15 percent of them, potentially hundreds of millions of dollars for many states and roughly $9 billion across all states — based on their error rates for fiscal year 2025 (which came out in June 2026) and 2026.

In its analysis, CBO estimated that states would collectively reduce or eliminate SNAP benefits for about 300,000 people in an average month over the 2028-2034 period, which essentially assumed that no impact from the cost shift mandate would occur until states needed to start paying the required share.

To be sure, exactly what actions states would take was harder for CBO to anticipate, compared to other reconciliation law changes that reduced eligibility or benefit levels but left the structure of the program unchanged. But as we’ve warned, the cost shift threatened harms that were both greater and more immediate than CBO estimated. With states’ 2025-2026 error rates being the basis for what they owe starting in 2028, states are incentivized to reduce error rates quickly, even at the cost of delaying or improperly denying benefits to eligible families — which isn’t counted as a payment error.

When states attempt to reduce errors by requiring substantially more paperwork, shortening certification periods, or adding more case reviews, they make the program more onerous to administer and more difficult for applicants to navigate. Especially in states where administrative capacity was already strained, this is causing delays in application processing, procedural denials, and other bureaucratic obstacles that are restricting access to SNAP. The impacts of those actions are felt across all types of households that use SNAP and may disproportionately affect seniors, people with disabilities, and working families, who may struggle to wait on hold for hours when calls go unanswered or to travel to a social services office during business hours for help with their paperwork.

And this all comes at a time when the economy’s prognosis is mixed at best. Year-over-year real wages have declined for six straight months (through September) and the unemployment rate has been flat since July 2025. In other words, it’s not likely the massive declines in SNAP participation are due to improving household finances and reduced need for help affording groceries.

Meanwhile, it’s likely that two other eligibility restrictions are only partially responsible for the decline in SNAP participation thus far and are not being fully felt yet. CBO’s cost estimate narrative for the 2025 reconciliation law predicted that together, these provisions will cause an average of 2.5 to 3 million people to lose SNAP eligibility altogether over the 2026-2034 budget window (and an average of fewer than 2 million people losing SNAP in 2026).

Taking SNAP away for not meeting a work requirement. The law dramatically expanded SNAP’s already harsh and ineffective work requirement, by extending it to older adults up to age 65 and to parents and other caregivers of children 14 and older. It also substantially narrowed states’ ability to waive the time limit for areas with few job opportunities and eliminated exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth. Research consistently shows the work requirement cuts many people off SNAP without increasing employment or earnings. CBO estimated this stricter work requirement would account for the greatest of the law’s cuts to SNAP participation: 2.4 million people on average over the 2025-2034 period. CBO assumed that this provision would begin to take effect in fiscal year 2026, when about 75 percent of the full annual impact would occur, meaning about 1.8 million people would be cut from SNAP in an average month in 2026.

Cutting eligibility for people who are immigrants. CBO estimated about 90,000 people would be cut from SNAP from the provision that denies SNAP to many people who are immigrants living lawfully in the U.S., having been granted humanitarian protections. There is emerging evidence that additional immigrants and their citizen family members have lost SNAP because of confusion over the rules and the climate of fear the Trump Administration has stoked around human services programs available to immigrants. But CBO did not assume such individuals would be cut from SNAP, and this likely represents a relatively small share of the decline in caseloads given that immigrants and citizens in mixed-status families represent a relatively small share of SNAP participants.

All told, SNAP losses will continue to mount due to the reconciliation law — including among people not targeted by the law, and in magnitudes CBO didn’t predict. At minimum Congress should delay the provision likely most responsible for early, outsized losses: the harmful state cost shift.

title: Todd Blanche Won’t Rule Out DOJ Disruption of Midterm Elections Certification
content:
Seven in 10 Americans don’t believe President Donald Trump will accept the midterm results.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters on Thursday that he wouldn’t rule out the possibility of the Department of Justice (DOJ) refusing to allow states to certify their own election results in this year’s midterm races.

Blanche’s comments come as Americans are expressing deep skepticism that President Donald Trump will accept election outcomes if Republicans lose to Democrats.

According to the U.S. Constitution, states are the managers of elections, not the federal government. But the administration could attempt to dispute the election results by claiming widespread fraud had taken place, refusing to allow states to certify outcomes through extreme measures, including seizing ballots.

author: Kenny Bruno
title: Mafia Diplomacy Will Continue After Kimberly Guilfoyle
content:
Guilfoyle’s mission in Greece — to push fossil fuels — is also playing out in the US with a permitting reform bill.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Kimberly Guilfoyle is out as U.S. ambassador to Greece. Mainstream media focused on Donald Trump Jr.’s former fiancée’s credit card bill and her penchant for extravagant partying and fashion. The next ambassador might not share those particular foibles, but the real significance of Guilfoyle’s appointment will last. She was what Dexter Filkins, writing in The New Yorker, calls “a new kind of Washington figure, for whom public office serves as a means to extraordinary wealth.” Donald Trump’s almost daughter-in-law was following in the footsteps of his son-in-law.

Jared Kushner does diplomacy and business simultaneously, and he’s getting really rich from it. While Kushner is dispatched to work on Iran and Ukraine, with meetings on the side to recruit billions to his investment funds, Guilfoyle was sent to Greece as the de facto ambassador for liquefied natural gas (LNG). In other words, her job was to shove LNG down the throats of Southeastern and Central European countries. Her refrain was U.S. energy dominance.

A more diplomatic diplomat might have noticed that one country’s dominance means, logically, another’s subservience. But tact was not Guilfoyle’s strong suit, and, according to the Wall Street Journal, another of her gaffes was not-so-subtly telling Greece’s energy minister that the U.S. could change the government of any country it wants.

Guilfoyle denies any intimidation took place, but threatening or forcing regime change for the sake of oil is not far-fetched. (See: Venezuela.)

In Southeast and Central Europe, the U.S. government is pushing something called the Vertical Gas Corridor (VGC), an opaque infrastructure initiative stretching from Greece through Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, Moldova, and ultimately Ukraine. As stated by the U.S. Energy Association, the VGC “opens access to Europe’s largest underground gas storage system, located in Ukraine.”

Publicly, the U.S. is framing the project as a strategic corridor that strengthens regional energy security and reduces Russian influence. In practice, it is becoming a way to trade dependence on Russia for dependence on the U.S. Greece will be the entry point and collaborator in the plan. U.S. LNG exporters stand to make huge profits, especially when there are high prices, as has been the case during the Iran War.

Why is the U.S. going to the mat for the Vertical Gas Corridor? The fossil fuel industry sees LNG exports as the lifeboat for the sinking ship of the conventional oil industry. For U.S. LNG, as with crude oil, it’s export or die. Those were Ambassador Guilfoyle’s marching orders.

An inconvenient reality for the industry is that market enthusiasm for the VGC appears remarkably weak. Repeated capacity auctions linked to the corridor, in which gas companies bid for the right to use pipelines and other infrastructure, have attracted limited commercial interest. Several auctions failed outright, while others generated only modest bookings concentrated in specific segments of the network.

Infrastructure projects backed by robust commercial fundamentals typically attract customers on their own merits, without the need for lobbying and strong-arming. Massive terminals require long-term contracts, and the U.S. is determined to get both — whether or not it makes any economic sense.

For Greece, the stakes are particularly high.

The country is being positioned as the southern gateway for American LNG entering Southeast Europe. While this positioning promises geopolitical visibility, it also risks tying the Greek economy to fossil fuel infrastructure whose long-term viability remains deeply uncertain. Investments in LNG terminals, pipelines, and associated facilities are dependent on future gas demand that may never materialize as Europe accelerates its clean-energy transition.

At the same time, communities and ecosystems in Greece bear the environmental costs, just as surely as the Texas and Louisiana communities where the methane gas originates. From the Sea of Thrace to other sensitive marine areas, new infrastructure developments are proceeding despite growing concerns over climate impacts, methane emissions, and ecological damage.

The Greek government’s response appears less like strategic energy planning and more like appeasement of the U.S. Greece assumes the financial risk of costly LNG terminals, pipeline expansions, and related infrastructure while being encouraged to lock itself and the wider region into decades-long gas contracts. The plan not only deepens dependence on a very unreliable and fickle U.S., but it exposes Greek citizens to long-term economic, geopolitical, and climate risks — all in service of U.S. exports.

Last year, during trade negotiations, the U.S. insisted that the EU buy a preposterous $750 billion in energy from the U.S. to avoid punishing tariffs. The EU capitulated. The U.S. is among the interested parties pressing the EU to delay its methane regulation, which is designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by excluding the dirtiest fuels from the EU market. The EU is capitulating on that as well.

In the U.S., for all the coverage of Guilfoyle’s clumsiness, there has been almost no attention to her true mission in Greece. It’s hidden, perhaps, because the take-our-gas-or-else approach is working on Capitol Hill as well. The permitting reform bill known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), meant to streamline permitting for both dirty fuels and clean energy, is one of the few pieces of legislation with supporters on both sides of the aisle. Yet the climate benefits of the bill are nil, because even though it will help the siting of wind and solar, it will help fossil fuels even more.

More clean energy doesn’t address climate change unless it replaces the burning of fossil fuels. In other words, the bill is likely to make emissions worse. Some proponents will rationalize that emissions will rise even more without the bill than with it. But playing to “lose by less” may not even work, because BAAJA will not only ease the way for fossil fuel permits but, in the name of certainty, will impede future U.S. administrations from transitioning off fossil fuels.

Even though it’s obviously a policy to lock in long-term commitment to oil and gas, some Democratic senators, and even climate champs, including Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, are supporting the bill. What’s maddening is that these senators surely understand that the only known method for addressing climate change at a large scale is to reduce the burning of fossil fuels. In the name of compromise, they are essentially giving up their cause — as if the floods, fires, storms, landslides, diseases, and other miseries caused by global heating will understand the need to accommodate a militantly pro-oil, anti-renewables government that does not negotiate in good faith. And they are doing so at a moment of minimum leverage, because their bargaining position is likely to be stronger after the next Congress is seated.

The United States is in a period of authoritarian rule, and Buy-Our-Gas-Or-Else is high on the agenda. The next U.S. Ambassador to Greece will understand the job is to communicate the demand for subservience, even if they pay their own credit card bills. The question is whether Greece, or the EU as a whole, or the Democrats in Congress, will stand up to it.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Hegseth Makes Unannounced Visit to Netanyahu Ahead of Israel’s Elections
content:
The visit came amid discussions between the US and Israel about a renewed assault on Iran.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday and met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, just eight days before Israel’s upcoming elections.

On Tuesday, in comments to reporters back in the U.S., Hegseth said that he was there “visiting our troops” and “had a chance to talk to the prime minister,” but that he would not discuss the subject of their meeting.

Hegseth met Netanyahu at the Ovda Air Base in southern Israel.

The visit comes amid discussions between the U.S. and Israel about a renewed assault on Iran. According to The Financial Times, Netanyahu had sought to launch a renewed attack on Iran earlier in October, but Trump dissuaded the attack, stating that it should not occur before the U.S. midterm elections. Hegseth, however, is reportedly among the strongest supporters of renewed strikes on Iran.

Hegseth’s visit came a day after Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October 27 elections. In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so.”

But Trump’s endorsement is unlikely to secure a majority for Netanyahu, who has been in power for 19 years — the longest of any Israeli prime minister — and is now facing a highly contested election. According to polling data, the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar Party is expected to win the most seats in Israel’s election next Tuesday, though no party is expected to secure a majority.

To form a governing coalition, the party with the most seats will need to form a coalition alongside other, smaller parties. But Eisenkot has stated that he would not form a government with Palestinian parties, particularly the Joint List.

In fact, Eisenkot’s “opposition” alliance diverges very little from Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party, particularly when it comes to Palestinians. Eisenkot has announced that he plans to continue to build Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, and that he is against a Palestinian state. He has even attempted to position himself to the right of Netanyahu on issues like the E1 settlement project, claiming that Netanyahu has been an obstacle to the project. Eisenkot has also stated his aim to expand the Israeli military by compelling Haredi Jews and Palestinian citizens of Israel to enlist in the army.

Tamir Sorek, professor at Penn State University, said in a recent Institute of Middle East Understanding press briefing that the anti-Netanyahu coalition “shares the same fantasy” of eliminating Palestinians, though “they refuse to articulate it.”

While Netanyahu’s Likud is more consistent and adamant in its attempts to exclude Palestinians from the electoral system, opposition parties like Eisenkot’s have also maneuvered to exclude the Palestinian parties, and to prevent Palestinian citizens of Israel — who make up 20 percent of Israel’s population — from voting.

The United Arab List, however, is seen as more acceptable by Israeli political parties than the Joint List, which consists of the more left-wing parties of Hadash (Jabha in Arabic), Ta’al, and Balad. The Arab List became the first Palestinian party to join an Israeli government in 2021, when Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid briefly removed Netanyahu from power.

But according to Sorek, a significant difference is that anti-Netanyahu voters are more sensitive to international pressure. “The question of who will be the next prime minister of Israel is secondary to whether the international community will press for sanctions on Israel,” Sorek asserted.

author: Tariq Ra’ouf
title: We Beat the Trump Administration in Court. Now We’re Going to the ICC.
content:
I am beginning to see a glimmer of hope that justice will be found for the dozens of family members I have lost in Gaza.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Over the course of the last three years, my family has lost 49 family members in Gaza. Their bodies were torn apart by shrapnel, crushed by falling buildings, and mutilated by bullets and munitions made and provided by the United States of America. Now, the U.S. is trying to dismantle the International Criminal Court, the only international court that can criminally prosecute U.S. officials for aiding and enabling genocide, by sanctioning the Court and attempting to intimidate anyone, including U.S. citizens, from working with them. So, in response, I joined others to sue this administration in order to take them to the very court they’re trying to destroy.

I’m a Palestinian-American organizer, and I helped establish Taxpayers Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG), which recently partnered with Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN) to sue the Trump administration so we can continue much-needed legal and advocacy work. Over the course of over a year, TAAG worked with an international legal team to prepare evidence against top U.S. officials for aiding and enabling the genocide of my people, but up until now, we haven’t been able to submit our evidence to the ICC because of this administration’s attacks and sanctions on the court and its judges.

Thankfully, that will now change after we successfully challenged the Trump administration in court. On October 13 we won a preliminary injunction that blocks this administration from being able to target our groups for working with sanctioned parties, clearing the way for us to proceed to the ICC. For the first time since the genocide started, I am beginning to see a glimmer of hope that justice will be found for the dozens of family members I have lost in Gaza.

Long before the Trump administration sanctioned the entirety of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on October 9, it first enacted Executive Order 14203 in February of 2025. This executive order granted administration officials the ability to sanction foreign nationals for supporting the ICC’s investigations into U.S. and Israeli parties guilty of committing war crimes and their complicity in genocide. Under this Executive Order (EO), the Trump administration also sanctioned leading Palestinian human rights groups al-Haq, al-Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights (PCHR), as well as the UN Special Rapporteur for the Human Rights Situation on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Francesca Albanese, along with other ICC officials.

What many people don’t know is that the EO that allowed the administration to sanction these parties doesn’t only go after foreign nationals, it also makes it a federal offense — punishable by a $1 million fine and/or 20 years in prison — for anyone, including American citizens, who provides or receives a “service” to or from a sanctioned party. This provision of the EO is exactly why TAAG and DAWN took this administration to court: Our lawsuit argued that the EO violates our First Amendment rights as American citizens to speak, associate, and engage in Palestine-related human rights advocacy with these parties. As a founding member of TAAG, I can tell you firsthand how these sanctions have prevented us and organizations like DAWN from being able to continue our work sharing evidence and advocacy ideas with people like Albanese and ICC officials, because the definition of “service” is so broad and undefined — the US can interpret it as being anything that confers a benefit to the recipient.

In an October 9 video of Marco Rubio announcing the actions against the ICC, he tries defending the administration’s actions by calling the ICC a “rogue court,” which the U.S. is “not subject to the jurisdiction of.” But Rubio leaves out a fundamental principle of international law: A country does not have to join the ICC for its nationals to fall within the Court’s jurisdiction.

If a country that is not a State Party to the Rome Statute commits a war crime on the lands of a country that is a state party, the perpetrator of that crime can be investigated. Given that Palestine is a State Party to the Rome Statute, and that Gaza (and the West Bank) are classified as Occupied Palestinian Territories by the United Nations, the ICC has every right to investigate and prosecute the United States and Israel for the insurmountable war crimes committed against my family members and thousands of other innocent civilians.

It is clear that the only “protections” this administration are seeking are for the citizens responsible for aiding and abetting war crimes, which after three years, we have plenty of evidence of. Anthony Aguilar, a retired US special forces officer and whistleblower who resigned from his work with the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) aid distribution centers in Gaza, has gone on record saying he saw the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) shooting at crowds of Palestinians, and in an interview with the BBC says he saw Israeli and American military forces of the GHF using an “indiscriminate and unnecessary force against a civilian population, an unarmed, starving population.”

Rubio consistently mentions the idea of “protecting American citizens” from investigations by the ICC, but the citizens he is referring to are the ones committing the war crimes he doesn’t want investigated. What about American citizens whose families have been killed with U.S.-supplied weapons? Who protects our right to seek justice?

In sanctioning the entirety of the ICC, the Trump administration is not only trying to cripple any attempt to hold them accountable for their war crimes, but they’re also telling American citizens like myself that if you dare to seek justice for the family members you’ve lost, we’ll imprison you.

Now that the courts sided with us in our lawsuit, we are finally able to prepare for the next steps ahead.

With the injunction in place, TAAG is now moving forward to finalize its evidence submission and plans to imminently send this to the ICC. We are also rallying support, within the US and beyond, for human rights organizations and advocates for the ICC to act responsibly upon this massive collection of evidence, in hopes that more parties take appropriate legal actions where possible. We fundamentally believe that grassroots movements like ours, and so many throughout the world, are the ones who must step up where our leadership has failed, and build the democratic, popular power capable of ensuring that legal action against genocide is taken and enforced.

We also hope that our actions inspire more American citizens to speak up against this administration and the priorities of our government. I helped found Taxpayers Alliance Against Genocide because I’m sick of our tax dollars being used against my own family in Gaza, while our communities here in the U.S. suffer from a lack of housing, education and healthcare. Those of us within TAAG recognize that we have a duty as American citizens to hold our nation accountable for the war crimes they commit, not just in Gaza but all over the world. We will not rest until we’ve exhausted every avenue to seek justice and accountability for these war crimes. We will continue collecting evidence, and pursuing every available legal avenue, moving forward with our crucial evidence work for a prospective submission to the ICC and advance our efforts to hold U.S. officials accountable for crimes against humanity. We will not be intimidated into abandoning our work, our families, or the principle that no one is above the law.

author: Jon Queally
title: Netanyahu Orders “Full Lockdown” of Occupied West Bank
content:
Smotrich said the Palestinian Authority should be “dismantled” and called for increased demolition of Palestinian homes.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that he has ordered the Israel Defense Force to “immediately impose a lockdown on Hebron and prepare for a full lockdown of the entire” illegally occupied West Bank following a gun battle that reportedly left two Palestinians dead and at least five Israeli soldiers wounded.

Following an emergency meeting with Israel’s security cabinet and his top military advisors, Netanyahu posted a statement to social media in which he blamed Hamas for the incident and accused the group of “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians.”

Netanyahu claimed that “large quantities of weapons and ammunition” had been discovered, but did not offer details about the nature of attack or its alleged planning.

Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who was on the scene of the shooting incident soon after it occurred, warned that “comprehensive military operation” in the occupied West Bank would soon be underway to handle those termed “terrorists.”

Smotrich also said that the Palestinian Authority, which governs the illegally occupied territories, should be “dismantled,” called for large-scale military operations like those executed in Gaza and Lebanon, and for the increased demolition of Palestinian homes.

“There is no alternative to a comprehensive military operation in Judea and Samaria that will lead to the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority, the confiscation of weapons and the elimination of terrorists,” Smotrich said. “Just as in Gaza and Lebanon.”

The order to demolish homes near where Friday’s incident took place, he added, “will begin to be implemented within the next hour, and the demolitions will continue throughout the afternoon.”

Mustafa Barghouti, founder and leader of the Palestinian National Initiative (PNI), was among those warning that what comes next will not be good for the Palestinian people, calling the complete closure of the West Bank “an act of collective punishment.”

Netanyahu, Barghouti said, “declared today that he is planning to carry out the ethnic cleansing of entire neighborhoods in Hebron.”

Such a declaration, he continued, “represents an alarming escalation in Israel’s policies of forced displacement and a flagrant violation of international law and the fundamental rights of the Palestinian people. It must be unequivocally condemned, and the international community must act immediately to prevent the forcible displacement of Palestinian residents and hold those responsible accountable.”

Yariv Oppenheimer, former director of Peace Now and a project director at the Geneva Institute, told Al-Jazeera in a Friday interview that Israeli leaders would now leverage the incident to further tighten their grip on the occupied West Bank, already rife with violence from Israeli settlers and IDF operations in Occupied Palestinian Territories (OPT).

“The Israeli army is getting into the Palestinian cities, the settlers are attacking Palestinians, and the situation is impossible” in the OPT, Oppenheimer explained.

Oppenheimer added that he expected Netanyahu and his cabinet to take advantage of this attack on Israeli soldiers in order to push “more propaganda” to justify the likely violence that is coming from the Israeli government and violent settler factions.

“There will be house demolitions. We will see [a] curfew. We will see more soldiers […] making arrests, and definitely we might see the settlers trying to target Palestinians in revenge for this attack, and trying to take advantage of this situation in order to escalate the situation even more,” Oppenheimer warned.

author: Marianne Dhenin
title: Tenants Unions Anticipate Housing Policy Gains After Progressives Win in RI
content:
Reclaim Rhode Island demonstrates the power of tenant organizing to effect change in local politics.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The housing crisis emerged as a central issue last month in Providence, Rhode Island, as Democratic socialist David Morales unseated incumbent Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary for mayor and a slate of progressives won their city council races in primaries throughout the Ocean State’s largest city.

In April, Smiley vetoed a rent stabilization ordinance passed the day before, and a month later the city council came up one vote short of overriding his veto.

“The campaign for rent stabilization and Brett Smiley’s veto of it laid the whole framework and groundwork for both David Morales’s race and the council slate,” said Daniel Denvir, co-chair at Reclaim Rhode Island, a member-led housing justice and progressive organizing group that is driving the growth of the Rhode Island Tenants Union. “It was a race around rent stabilization and with a clear mandate to pursue social housing — and we won every single contested race in the city. Now, Providence will be really an unparalleled site for innovative progressive solutions to the housing crisis.”

Reclaim grew out of connections organizers made working on the 2020 Bernie Sanders campaign in Rhode Island and has had some major successes organizing tenant unions across Providence County and in fighting to ban practices that drive rent hikes and profit for landlords, like algorithmic rent setting. One of its biggest wins in the tenant organizing sphere came this June when residents at Charles Place launched their union with supermajority support, becoming the largest chapter of the Rhode Island Tenants Union. The 200-unit apartment block is home to Section 8 tenants, many of whom are aging or disabled. The union has forced the building’s landlord to the table to negotiate an agreement expected to fix persistent problems, including broken air conditioners, an unreliable elevator, and absent management.

After the rent stabilization ordinance in Providence was quashed and an earlier Reclaim-backed effort to protect tenants from unreasonable evictions by codifying just-cause eviction at the state level failed, the organization shifted some of its efforts to organizing around progressive candidates who could help overcome institutional barriers to its just housing agenda in the legislature.

The City of Providence is among the nation’s least affordable for renters. Last year, the city council’s housing crisis task force found that almost half of the city’s renters are spending beyond their means on housing.

“It’s a working-class city, it’s a diverse city, it’s a young city, it’s an artistic and bohemian city, and the unaffordability of housing threatens all of those things that make Providence special,” Denvir told Truthout. “That’s an objective social and economic reality, [and] the role of political organizations like Reclaim Rhode Island is to organize the objective crisis into a collective political response that brings people together to exercise collective power to solve that crisis.”

With progressives expected to hold a majority, if not a supermajority, on Providence City Council after the general election, local organizers are looking forward to implementing the solutions they fought for on the campaign trail.

While candidates were campaigning ahead of Providence’s September 9 primaries, Reclaim fielded about 200 volunteers who knocked on thousands of doors on joint canvasses for Morales and progressive city council candidates. “We won this on the doors,” said Miguel Martínez Youngs, who defeated incumbent John Goncalves by 68 votes in the Democratic primary in Ward 1. Youngs will run unopposed in the general election on November 3.

Ward 1 includes downtown Providence and historic neighborhoods where residents have faced waves of gentrification and displacement. It also includes College Hill, home to Brown University and one of the city’s most affluent neighborhoods. Goncalves has represented the district since 2020 and bills himself as a progressive. But he was also a deciding factor that saw Smiley’s veto of the rent stabilization ordinance stand when he opted not to show up for the vote to override it. “I got good on the campaign trail saying, ‘It wasn’t a no vote, it was a no show — which is worse,’” Youngs told Truthout.

It was a move that fired up Goncalves’s eventual opponents. “We mounted a really hardcore campaign to try to get that veto overturned but fell one vote short,” Denvir told Truthout. “In the process, we issued a clear warning to Goncalves that if he did not support rent stabilization, we would primary him, defeat him, and end his political career.”

Goncalves spent about $160,000 on his campaign in the year leading up to the September 9 primary. Youngs told Truthout that, in contrast, his campaign spent about $30,000, raised through small-dollar donations. But Goncalves’s spending was no match for the people power that Youngs tapped into, including volunteer canvassers from Reclaim and RIFT/AFT Local 6516, a union of graduate student workers at Brown University, as well as endorsements from other local labor unions and Rhode Island Working Families Party.

“I had days where there were like 40 or 50 people going out for me, and we literally covered the whole ward — and that was such a sign,” Youngs told Truthout. “It was inspiring in my campaign the way that progressivism fell back on [its] roots, to people coming out.”

Reclaim also mobilized its network of organized tenants to help propel Morales and his allies to wins last month. Caleb Madison, Reclaim’s organizing director, said Morales differentiated himself by offering real fixes for common problems facing low-income tenants.

“A lot of politicians use Section 8 tenants in high-rise buildings as vote farms,” Madison told Truthout. “They’ll show up there once every three or four years for their reelection campaign, give everybody coffee and donuts and say why they should vote for them. Meanwhile, Morales comes through with an actual grounded plan about ways to improve their lives — things like more building inspections, more code violations, more people to call. That’s what really inspired tenants to show up for Morales.”

Similar messaging is resonating with voters elsewhere, too, as the housing affordability crisis deepens nationwide. Zohran Mamdani’s upset victory in last year’s New York City mayoral race rested in part on his promise to freeze rents for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments. This election cycle, left-wing candidates running on implementing or expanding rent control, curbing corporate development, or other measures to support tenants have also seen success in races as diverse as Washington, D.C. City Council, a congressional seat in central Michigan, and one of Florida’s seats in the U.S. Senate.

Denvir told Truthout the wins reflect the fact that housing affordability has become a “profound crisis to which only the left is offering a compelling response.”

Now, with progressives expected to hold a majority, if not a supermajority, on Providence City Council after the general election, local organizers are looking forward to implementing the solutions they fought for on the campaign trail. Morales has committed to working with the Providence City Council to pass and enforce rent stabilization within his first 100 days using the model developed under the outgoing council, which would cap rent increases to a maximum of 4 percent in a 12-month period. Morales has also said he plans to task the city’s redevelopment agency with acquiring vacant buildings and empty lots to transform them into permanently affordable homes.

Youngs, who helped draft Providence’s rent stabilization ordinance in his previous role as deputy director of policy for the Providence City Council, said he sees his job as an incoming city councilor as having two parts: First, he’s committed to delivering on the day-to-day needs of his constituents — from repairing broken streetlamps to installing a new bench at the neighborhood bus stop. Second, he wants to help ensure Morales can follow through on promises to the city’s tenants. “My goal is to be someone on council who’s trying to whip a council together that could be as supportive of the mayor [as possible] and making sure that we take care of my priorities, and rent stabilization is on the top of my list,” he told Truthout.

“On the municipal level, you can swing these elections by 100 or 200 votes — that’s one union being able to flip direct control of the city. If we can get more and more tenants into these unions, they will have more and more ability to decide who is in or out of office and who actually is going to speak to their needs.”

With pro-tenant changes all but assured in Providence, Denvir told Truthout that Reclaim’s advocacy arm may once again set its sights on the state legislature. “It’s quite possible that we return to the State House, now that Providence has clearly shown the power of the organized working class and the left in Rhode Island, to insist that we get just-cause eviction done,” he said.

The organization’s tenant organizing work will continue as well, and Madison told Truthout he hopes organizers in other cities will take a page from Reclaim’s book and recognize the power of tenant organizing to effect change, especially in local politics. “On the municipal level, you can swing these elections by 100 or 200 votes — that’s one union being able to flip direct control of the city,” he told Truthout. “If we can get more and more tenants into these unions, they will have more and more ability to decide who is in or out of office and who actually is going to speak to their needs.”

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Critic Louise Lucas Indicted as DOJ Ignores Election-Year Guidelines
content:
“I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now,” said Virginia State Sen. Louise Lucas.

On Thursday, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a slew of charges against Virginia State Sen. author: Jessica Corbett
title: Trump’s Justice Department Ditches Civil Rights and School Desegregation Cases
content:
“Walking away from them doesn’t mean the discrimination has been addressed,” points out a former agency official.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A pair of papers published Thursday by the legal group Democracy Forward detail how, under President Donald Trump, the Department of Justice has dumped dozens of cases focused on school desegregation and the civil rights of people of color, all while weaponizing the DOJ to serve “the most dangerous criminal in US history” and his allies.

The cases were previously taken up by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, currently led by Harmeet Dhillon, whose confirmation was controversial — like those of Trump’s first attorney general for this term, Pam Bondi, whom he fired in April and replaced with his former personal lawyer, Todd Blanche.

The new analyses of the cases — “Walking Away: DOJ’s Abandonment of Civil Rights Cases for People of Color” and “Filling in The Gaps: Tracking The 50+ School Desegregation Cases DOJ Says It Is Ending” — were developed by Democracy Forward’s oversight and accountability project Red Line for Civil Rights.

“People and communities rely on DOJ to pursue vital cases to address threats to civil rights under our nation’s laws. The Red Line for Civil Rights reports don’t just highlight the cases that have been abandoned, but also make clear the harm that DOJ’s abandonment of its mission retreat has caused,” said Democracy Forward president and CEO Skye Perryman.

The project found at least 36 abandoned cases and probes addressing discrimination against Black, Latino, and Native American people, from Voting Rights Act lawsuits and redlining settlements with banks to firefighter and police hiring issues.

There was United States v. Cobb County, Georgia, in which the DOJ alleged that credit checks and a written exam illegally screened out Black firefighter applicants, and United States v. Patriot Bank, a 2024 consent order over redlining of Black and Hispanic neighborhoods in Memphis, Tennessee.

In United States v. SouthEast Bank, the department argued that a student loan refinancing product discriminated against Alaska Native, American Indian, and Black applicants, and in United States v. City of Minneapolis, the DOJ concluded that police discriminated against Black and Native American in Minnesotans.

“The shameful withdrawal of DOJ resources from these cases and investigations highlights how this administration is abandoning communities across the country,” said Megan Marks, a former leader in the department who is now the project’s deputy director and managing editor. “Walking away from them doesn’t mean the discrimination has been addressed. It just means DOJ is no longer watching.”

In its second analysis, the project identified 56 school districts in 12 states where the department has moved to ditch or end a desegregation case, or did not oppose ending one — from Athens City, Alabama and Chesterfield County, South Carolina to South Bend, Indiana and Waterbury, Connecticut.

“The Supreme Court held in its landmark 1954 case, Brown v. Board of Education, that segregating public school students by race violates the 14th Amendment’s guarantee of equal protection,” the report notes. “Since Brown, DOJ has monitored and enforced desegregation orders, reviewing evidence and often working collaboratively with school districts and, in some cases, private plaintiffs to support progress.”

“This work was central to the Civil Rights Division’s history. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 authorized DOJ to file its own school desegregation lawsuits against public schools or institutions of higher education and to join cases that families had already brought,” the paper explains. “These school desegregation cases are how the promise of Brown reaches individual classrooms. Behind each of these cases are children, families, and a community that fought, sometimes at great personal risk, for the right to an equal education.”

Shaheena Simons previously oversaw the Justice Department’s desegregation docket but is now a senior adviser at the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. In response to the report, she said that the “DOJ’s haste to end these cases without deliberation or transparency is a betrayal of Black students who continue to face segregation and inequality in our schools.”

“This retreat is part of a much bigger picture,” Simons emphasized. “Not only has the Civil Rights Division abandoned its work to protect the rights of our most marginalized students, but it is also weaponizing civil rights statutes against them.”

Democratic leaders in the US House of Representatives also spoke out about the project’s findings. Education and Workforce Committee Ranking Member Bobby Scott (Va.) accused the “politicized” department of “turning its back on workers and students by abandoning entire categories of discrimination cases and ending the fight against school desegregation altogether.”

Democrats on his panel “are committed to the protection of civil rights and to guaranteeing that all Americans are protected from discrimination in accordance with the civil rights laws that so many Americans fought to secure,” pledged Scott, as his party prepares for next month’s midterm elections, in which Republicans could lose control of one or both chambers of Congress.

Fellow Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin (Md.), a constitutional scholar and ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, said that “Democracy Forward’s reports expose the Justice Department’s shocking betrayal of its central duty to protect Americans against race discrimination.”

“While DOJ devotes its resources to persecuting Trump’s political enemies, it has dropped protection of voting rights and is allowing discrimination to proliferate by abandoning school desegregation and job discrimination cases,” he said, as the Trump administration pursues everyone from former Federal Bureau of Investigation Director James Comey to New York Attorney General Letitia James and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).

“We need a Department of Justice that stands by the rule of law and the rights of all Americans,” Raskin asserted. “But this administration carries out presidential vendettas, covers up child sex trafficking, promotes corruption, and pardons and coddles violent felons in the president’s private militia.”

author: Sara Luterman
title: Nursing Home Residents Have a Right to Vote — Despite What Trump CMS Agency Says
content:
The Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Cindy Napolitan and her daughter Melissa have multiple sclerosis, a degenerative condition in which the immune system attacks the brain, spinal cord and nerves. They have lived together at a nursing home in Mesquite, Texas, for nine years. In previous elections, Cindy and Melissa Napolitan voted by mail, but this year they took an unusual step: They voted in person. They worried their mail-in ballots — and even their in-person votes — may not be counted.

“I’ve never worried like this before. I’ve never worried that I don’t have the proper ID. I’ve never worried that somebody is going to intimidate me. Will I encounter somebody that’s going to threaten me or make me feel less than? So yeah, I’m very worried, and I shouldn’t be,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I shouldn’t have to be worried about stuff like that. This is the 19th Amendment. I’m allowed to vote.”

Nursing home residents are guaranteed the right to vote. Around two-thirds of all nursing home residents in the United States are women, making aging and long-term care gendered issues.

There is no data on how many nursing home residents exercise that right. Cindy, 70, and Melissa Napolitan, 48, at least, feel like they’ve had good experiences with voting at their facility. Cindy Napolitan, in particular, has worked with the activities coordinator to organize rides to the polls for her, her daughter and other interested residents.

“We are scheduled to go on the first day of early voting. So in case there are any issues that we come across, we still have time to rectify the situation and be allowed to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan are more concerned this year than in previous years about government interference and voter suppression. Their fears are not unfounded: Experts and advocates for the rights of nursing home residents, older adults and people with disabilities are worried too.

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rescinded previous guidance affirming that nursing home residents have the right to vote.

“The memo does not alter the underlying law. Nursing homes are governed by the Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 and its implementing regulations,” said Nina Kohn, a professor at Syracuse University and expert on elder law. “That law still requires facilities to support their residents in exercising their rights as Americans.”

The memo also emphasized voter fraud in nursing homes, specifically around mail-in ballots. For years, President Trump has disparaged mail-in ballots, insisting without evidence that fraudulent votes by mail had a role in his loss during the 2020 presidential election. His comments have led to some states restricting who can use a mail-in ballot and in what contexts.

According to experts, including Kohn, there is no evidence that voter fraud is a serious or widespread problem in nursing homes. Instead, Kohn is concerned about the chilling effect that it may have on residents’ rights.

“The language in the memo itself is intimidating, and it may understandably make staff think that they could face criminal prosecution or be in some other form of legal trouble if they help residents vote,” Kohn said.

Cindy and Melissa Napolitan do everything together — and on Monday, they voted together. They are also roommates at the facility; most people living in nursing homes are assigned roommates who are strangers.

“Unlike other people that have roommates that don’t get along, I’m very lucky and fortunate that I have somebody that loves me and I love her,” Cindy Napolitan said.

This is the second time Cindy and Melissa Napolitan have voted in person since entering a nursing home. The first time was during the 2024 presidential election.

“I’ve been checking my status weekly to make sure that I haven’t been dropped off the voter rolls, making sure my daughter and I don’t have some sort of issue that says that we can’t vote,” Cindy Napolitan said.

People living in nursing homes and other long-term care facilities face specific barriers. Some residents may need assistance filling out their ballots because they lack the movement or dexterity to hold a pen or press buttons on a computer screen. People with dexterity or coordination issues may also be unable to produce the same signature twice.

“With some forms of voting, some states will use your ID to verify your signature. If your signature looks different than the one on your ID, your ballot might get thrown out. Or there is a ballot hearing process, so you could be notified of that and able to fix it, but it is a bunch of extra steps that impact disabled voters at higher rates,” said Alexia Kemerling, director of Accessible Democracy for the nonpartisan American Association of People with Disabilities.

An increasing number of states now require voters to show some form of photo identification. This can also be a problem for many nursing home residents because they may no longer have a driver’s license. They also may no longer have passports because they aren’t traveling internationally. States have other forms of identification, but getting them can involve complex paperwork and multiple trips.

Some states will accommodate voters in nursing homes and other facilities so they can acquire state identification that isn’t a driver’s license.

“My license expired, and so I had to apply for an identification card. I had to coordinate with them to come here instead of going to the DMV because I wasn’t about to do that. I didn’t know how long I would have to sit there. I didn’t have a ride,” Melissa Napolitan said. “They came and took our pictures, and filled out all the forms for us.”

Kemerling objects to the idea that this somehow renders nursing home residents and other people with disabilities incapable of making an independent choice.

“In the disability community, we don’t necessarily mean that independence means doing something alone. Independence is having control over how something is done,” Kemerling said. “Just because you need someone to assist you as part of the voting process does not mean that you are giving up your choice.”

There are steps nursing home residents and their families can take to advocate for their rights. Lori Smetanka is the executive director of the National Consumer Voice for Quality Long Term Care, which advocates on behalf of people living in nursing homes and assisted living facilities. Her organization produces a fact sheet for nursing home residents enumerating their rights and how they can advocate for themselves.

“For the generation of people that are living in long-term care facilities, it’s largely an older population of people,” Smetanka said. “It’s very important to them to exercise their right to vote. When we talk with residents, it is very important to them. Some of them have really advocated very heavily for themselves in order to be able to do that.”

Smetanka emphasized that it is not only up to residents and their families to advocate for their rights.

“If the resident has the ability to raise the questions about it, they certainly should be doing that, Smetanka said. “Families should be asking, but staff should be asking too — ‘What can we do to help you vote this year? Who is interested in voting? How can we get the requirements in place so you can cast your ballots?’” At some facilities, voting may not be on staff’s radar, despite the legal requirements.

Cindy Napolitan has been active in advocating for her right to vote, as well as the rights of her fellow residents, and she encourages others who are able to do the same.

“I’m very vocal and very into advocating for our residents here and making sure that they’re all able to vote,” Cindy Napolitan said. “I’m the one that will start telling our activity director that there’s a deadline for filing to become a registered voter. There’s a deadline to file for a mail-in ballot, and I’m usually the one that makes sure that those things get done.”

When asked what she wants people to understand most about voting in nursing homes, Melissa Napolitan pushed back against the insinuation that nursing homes are hotbeds of voter fraud and that she and her peers don’t have their own opinions.

“I think that people maybe don’t take the time to realize that people in nursing homes aren’t just here waiting to die,” Melissa Napolitan said.
