author: Chris Walker
title: Acton Says Ramaswamy Exploited Her Estranged Mother for Political Gain
content:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton accused her mother’s then-husband of sexual assault when she was a child.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Democratic candidate for Ohio governor Amy Acton has responded to a political ad produced by her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign, which features her mother — whom she’s been estranged from for decades — describing Acton as a liar.

The ad is being widely criticized as distasteful because Acton accused her mother and her then-stepfather of abuse and sexual assault when she was just a child.

In the ad, Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, is shown speaking directly into the camera about her daughter, whom she has not seen since 1978, when Acton was just 12 years old.

“Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar,” Arthur says. “She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help.”

The ad doesn’t mention why Arthur believes her daughter is a liar, and it leaves out all relevant information about their estrangement.

Acton alleges that she was the victim of sexual abuse by Arthur’s now-deceased husband when she was between the ages of 10 and 12. Acton has also recalled being unhoused at one point while living with her mother and stepfather.

She later told her father about the abuses, and a grand jury indicted her stepfather. Her mother and stepfather then fled the state to avoid prosecution, Acton has recounted.

The ad did not indicate who paid for or produced it. Though the Ramaswamy campaign had initially avoided taking responsibility for the ad, it has now admitted they made the commercial. What’s more, the campaign intends to spend an additional $4 million to continue airing it.

The campaign defended the ad in a statement.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor,” the Ramaswamy campaign said.

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance came to Ramaswamy’s defense.

“Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” Vance said in response to a reporter’s question, saying he was more focused on the election’s outcome.

“Have the opinion you want to have on that ad,” Vance continued, adding that he was “disgusted” at members of his own party “whining” about the contents of the ad.

Acton has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad in a statement posted on Facebook.

“Between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me. … I’ve always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it’s sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain,” Acton said.

I know what it feels like to be a child who is hungry, frightened, and uncertain of what tomorrow will bring. I know what it means to feel powerless and to depend on the courage and compassion of others to find a way forward. Those experiences shaped my values, my compassion, and my belief that every person deserves to be safe, to be heard, and to have a fair chance at a better life. They are part of what led me to become a doctor, to dedicate my life to public service, and to fight for people who too often feel forgotten or left behind.

Acton’s brother, Phillip Stearns, has also blasted the ad.

As a nurse in the neonatal intensive care unit, Jean Stone knows what it really means to live in a country with no paid parental leave.

author: Blanca Missé
title: As More Unions Oppose ICE and Israel, the Right Is Cracking Down
content:
The right is trying to gain access to labor unions’ minutes, membership lists, and Zoom chats.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On September 22, The Free Press attacked the California Faculty Association (CFA), which represents about 29,000 faculty, librarians, counselors, and coaches across the California State University (CSU) system. Drawing on private discussions about a proposed Jewish caucus, including communications from a union Zoom meeting, the article accused CFA of antisemitism. How those communications reached the publication remains unclear. Two days later, the Jewish Journal amplified those allegations, urging Gov. Gavin Newsom to consider them as he weighed California Assembly Bill (AB) 2551, CFA-sponsored legislation challenging campus protest restrictions imposed after the 2024 Palestine solidarity encampments. Less than a week after The Free Press story was published, Newsom vetoed the bill.

Pro-Israel and Jewish advocacy organizations had already campaigned against AB 2551 before the union’s internal deliberations were targeted, arguing that greater scrutiny would weaken rules needed to protect Jewish students from harassment and intimidation. Newsom’s veto does not prove coordination, but the campaign portraying CFA as hostile to Jewish students had become entangled with the union’s fight against campus protest restrictions.

The CSU’s systemwide policy prohibits encampments, overnight demonstrations, and unauthorized structures. The CSU Academic Senate immediately condemned the restrictions as undermining academic freedom when it was instituted in 2024, while CFA warned that vague definitions of disruption threatened constitutionally protected speech, assembly, protest, and future strike activity. A major 2026 ACLU-Amnesty study, investigating 80 campuses over two years, documented sweeping repression of Palestine solidarity protests. As the report found, universities “have imposed sweeping restrictions on student speech, initiated disciplinary actions against students, and imposed severe punishments, including expulsions and suspensions.” The ACLU has insisted that even legitimate time, place, and manner restrictions “must leave ample room for students to express themselves.”

The controversy reaches beyond CFA and CSU. Unions and rank-and-file organizations committed to Palestine solidarity have been forced to relitigate, again and again, whether anti-Zionism and solidarity with Palestinians constitute antisemitism — and whether such organizing should be systematically policed, investigated, or surveilled. At stake is a more fundamental right of the exploited: Can workers democratically connect economic struggles with Palestine solidarity, resistance to anti-immigrant and anti-Black racism, and the defense of civil liberties without exposing their organizing and deliberations to external pressure or repression?

We already have a word for the use of legal process as a political weapon: lawfare. You do not necessarily have to win. Investigation, expense, compelled disclosure, and possible sanctions can exact their own price.

Call its media counterpart pressfare: leaked material, selective or doctored quotations, and public identification can turn people into political targets and invite pressure on employers, universities, or government agencies.

The leaked CFA meeting should not be adjudicated through fragments selected for publication, especially when CFA’s statewide record contradicts the portrayal of a union indifferent to antisemitism. During the 2024 encampments, CFA opposed antisemitism and Islamophobia “in all forms” while supporting the encampments. Amid a 2025 federal antisemitism investigation, it stated that “as CFA members, we are united against antisemitism; it has no place in our communities,” while defending members’ academic freedom. CFA’s Palestine, Arab, and Muslim Caucus likewise defines its mission as confronting racism “in all its manifestations,” explicitly including antisemitism. The Free Press story — a clear example of pressfare — sought to overwrite this legacy with weaponized accusations, undermining the trust that workers place in the sanctity of their union spaces and processes.

Antisemitism demands to be taken seriously — which is why accusations of anti-Jewish discrimination should not be instrumentalized. Kenneth Stern, director of the Bard Center for the Study of Hate, has warned that using the International Holocaust Remembrance Association (IHRA) definition of antisemitism as a regulatory code threatens academic freedom by equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, while the Jerusalem Declaration warns that the definition’s ambiguities have generated confusion and controversy, “hence weakening the fight against antisemitism.” And as Jewish Voice for Peace and Jerusalem Declaration scholars have argued, combating antisemitism is not helped by conflating hostility toward Jews with anti-Zionism, criticism of Israel, or Palestine solidarity. Requiring Palestinian and anti-Zionist unionists to prove otherwise reverses the burden of proof, allowing accusations to substitute for evidence and cultivating fear and suspicion that inhibit collective action while fueling an ever-expanding search for evidence.

That ever-expanding search has taken the form of several federal antisemitism inquiries targeting universities and their workers.

Federal antisemitism investigations have extended scrutiny to faculty speech and Palestine solidarity organizing, with consequences for unions. At Cal State LA, CSU disclosed employees’ personal information to federal investigators, prompting CFA to sue over violations of workers’ privacy.

What drove these federal inquiries on antisemitism? A 2025 study from the American Association of University Professors and the Middle East Studies Association examined 102 complaints that prompted federal civil rights investigations; pro-Israel and right-wing organizations were involved in 78 percent. All but one of the complaints concerned speech critical of Israel, and in 80 percent, complainants characterized criticism of Israel or Zionism that made no reference to Jews or Judaism as antisemitic. In at least half, the complaint rested solely on constitutionally protected political speech.

The study separately examined 28 Title VI antisemitism lawsuits brought against universities by pro-Israel groups. As of its cutoff, not one had produced a final judicial finding of discrimination in favor of the plaintiffs, although some resulted in settlements imposing new restrictions on campus speech and protest.

CFA’s political commitments long predate the renewed Palestine solidarity movement. In 2023, the union challenged CSU administrators on First Amendment grounds for restricting classroom discussion of strikes. In 2020, after years of organizing, CFA helped secure passage of AB 1460, the landmark law making Ethnic Studies a graduation requirement across the CSU system — a major victory for racial justice and educational equity in one of the nation’s most racially and ethnically diverse states. Since then, it has continued fighting CSU over its implementation, defending faculty control over curriculum and the integrity of Ethnic Studies programs.

Now, at the bargaining table, CFA is seeking protections against retaliation for faculty speech, assembly, and protest through an academic freedom article that would make those protections enforceable through the union contract.

Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity?

The Free Press article published names and private union messages, exposing faculty, particularly faculty of color vulnerable around employment and tenure, to potential retaliation. Among those identified was Omar Zahzah, whose scholarship includes the book Terms of Servitude, on U.S. technology companies and Israeli settler colonialism. He had also recently written about the “Michigan 8,” warning of “a broader targeting of the pro-Palestine movement.” Whatever the intent, the chilling message is clear: Continue this scholarship, political writing, or union organizing, and you, too, risk public exposure and targeting.

The consequences of this attack reach into union democracy itself: Fear of exposure changes what members dare to say, whom they trust, and how they are willing to organize together. In 2025, CFA sued CSU after Cal State LA disclosed faculty and staff members’ personal contact information to federal investigators conducting an antisemitism inquiry. The union secured a January 2026 settlement requiring CSU to notify employees before complying with any specified federal demands for personal information, unless legally prohibited.

The exposure of CFA’s internal deliberations raises a question beyond leaked communications: Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity? In Minnesota and Michigan, that scrutiny has taken a more coercive form: undercover surveillance and federal subpoenas.

In Minnesota, federal agents infiltrated political meetings and activist chats under “Operation Puppet Master,” a surveillance operation exposed during the prosecution of the “Minnesota 15,” activists charged with conspiracy to impede federal officers. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) slide titled “The Conspiracy” mapped 18 organizations, including unions, while Homeland Security Investigations used administrative subpoenas — requiring no judicial approval — to obtain years of financial records connected to Service Employees International Union (SEIU) and Communications Workers of America (CWA). Defense attorney Kevin Riach challenged the surveillance as lacking any “articulable criminal predicate” and violating constitutional protections; federal prosecutors maintained that the charges concerned criminal conduct alone.

At a February workers’ assembly at Minneapolis’s United Labor Centre, roughly 400 workers debated labor’s response to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). One undercover agent reported “no real threats”; another sought to “get phone numbers.” Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration and whether anti-ICE activists were selectively prosecuted.

Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration.

In Michigan, following the indictment of the Michigan 8 — eight Palestine solidarity activists accused of conspiracy — a federal grand jury subpoena demanded Graduate Employees’ Organization (GEO) records dating to January 1, 2023: current and former membership information, officers, meeting minutes, personnel, and finances.

GEO President Hiab Teshome faced felony embezzlement and false-pretenses charges over alleged misuse of student organization funds. University police also sought to bar her from campus, potentially excluding a member of the union’s bargaining team from her workplace. Both charges were dismissed on August 6 — the day the federal subpoena was signed. GEO denounced the prosecution as politically motivated and moved to quash the subpoena. The dismissal does not establish a political motive behind the federal investigation, but the juxtaposition is striking: The charges against one union leader collapsed, yet federal scrutiny extended to the entire union — who belonged to GEO, who led it, what its members discussed, and how they spent their money.

Those records could reveal how solidarity was organized. Meanwhile, GEO says university management struck proposed contract language barring disclosure of workers’ union membership to the federal government. The constitutional stakes are hardly new: In the 1958 case of NAACP v. Alabama, the Supreme Court recognized that compelled disclosure of membership lists can expose people to retaliation and deter lawful political association.

Membership lists, meeting minutes, financial records, and private communications reveal who organizes with whom. Historian Ellen Schrecker identifies a disturbing historical precedent in McCarthyism’s system of “guilt by association”: Private groups compiled dossiers, government investigated political affiliations, and employers and universities imposed punishment. She sees today’s assault on higher education as even more dire: “Today, what’s happening is worse, so much worse that we have to really find a new phrase for it,” she told Democracy Now!.

Labor has its own answer to “guilt by association”: solidarity by association — where association is not a risk to be feared, but a means of repairing what injustice or oppression has torn apart. In the words of the Minnesota 15 solidarity campaign, “Community Is Not Conspiracy.” Rather than accept the social hierarchies that divide and oppress workers, union organizers build relationships that can dismantle and transform them. In organizing with those under attack, workers discover capacities for collective action that none could exercise alone. An injury to an immigrant family facing deportation, a Black community confronting police violence, or Palestinians facing repression thus becomes a concern for workers beyond those immediately targeted.

“An injury to one is an injury to all” means little if solidarity becomes competitive or selective — if defending Jewish workers requires silence about Palestinians, if defending citizens means abandoning undocumented workers, or if wages are labor’s concern while police violence, deportations, and attacks on civil liberties belong to somebody else.

Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate.

Union meetings, caucuses, and other forms of association create spaces where workers connect economic and political struggles, building solidarity across sectors rather than dividing struggles against racism, gender oppression, political repression, and exploitation into separate constituencies. Through these relationships, workers build collective power, expanding their capacity to think, feel, and act together beyond the narrow and isolated roles assigned to them in the workplace and, more broadly, under capitalism.

Yet none of this is possible without preserving unions’ internal democracy and political independence. Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate. Pressfare undermines that democracy when unproven allegations and internal deliberations become material for public targeting; lawfare erodes the independence of unions when accusations and investigations impose political costs before wrongdoing is established. Undercover agents mapping worker assemblies and prosecutors demanding years of union records bring far greater coercive power to bear on those same democratic spaces.

These methods differ in form and intensity, but they reproduce the same political effects: fear, suspicion, sadness, and isolation. These are effects that weaken the relationships through which workers might act together and change their circumstances. Solidarity, by contrast, nurtures compassion, courage, and the joy of gathering in assemblies, discovering what we can accomplish together. It strengthens our capacity not only to resist oppression and exploitation but to transform the social relations that sustain them. Perhaps that is what those who fear organized labor solidarity find most threatening.

title: Anthropic Proposes AI Bill With 50-Death Threshold Before Models Can Be Halted
content:
The company has reportedly been working with lawmakers on a lax regulatory model since the start of summer.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Anthropic, one of the major industry leaders in the development of artificial intelligence (AI), has proposed legislation for Congress that would provide a framework for regulating the technology, with strict limits on which government agencies can halt AI models, and narrow conditions under which regulation can occur.

Details of the proposal, which was not initially made public, were reported on Friday by Politico.

The bill would allow the federal government to block the release or continued operation of an AI model only if it poses an imminent risk. That risk, the proposal insists, must equal either $1 billion in financial damages or the possibility of AI modeling killing or seriously injuring at least 50 people.

Some observers argue that the very purpose of written judgments is to justify acts of violence. But one need not go that far to see the immediate effects: A judicial opinion can cause a death, ignite a civil war, legitimize a coup, or even wipe out an entire culture.

Cruikshank, an all-but-forgotten Reconstruction-era ruling. In Cruikshank, the Supreme Court held that the federal government could not prosecute the broad-daylight massacre of dozens of Black Republicans in 1873, most of whom were defending political offices duly won by their candidates. After two grueling trials and an unlikely guilty verdict by a Louisiana jury, the Court threw out the convictions.

A 56-year-old Mexican man held at a federal immigration facility in Laredo was found dead in his cell Saturday morning, his daughter and U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Laredo, confirmed to The Texas Tribune.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unresponsive by staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center during a security check at around 10 a.m. Saturday, Cuellar said. Staff performed CPR and called emergency services.

Craig Unit 1, a coal-fired power plant distinguished by tall exhaust smokestacks that rise above a rolling landscape in northwestern Colorado, was scheduled to close for good at the end of 2025 amid pressure from environmental advocates, public interest groups and state officials.

But on Dec. 30, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered it to keep burning coal. The unit had suffered a mechanical failure 11 days earlier and was not even running. Wright has since renewed the order three times — most recently on Sept. 25, extending the plant’s life through Christmas Day, a full year past its retirement date.

Its operator, Tri-State Generation and Transmission, is a nonprofit rural cooperative, and in January it joined co-owner Platte River Power Authority, a public power agency, in arguing that Wright’s orders violate the Constitution and federal law — a fight that has since reached a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. Before October 7, 2023, during my fourth year in university, I used to visit a bookshop in Gaza City to buy English novels for enhancing my linguistic link with my job and the students. In 2022, shortly before I graduated, I wrote a short story about our tough conditions in Gaza and submitted it to a writing competition. It ranked seventh out of 80 stories, and I received a reward. More than 100,000 Ukrainians and roughly 2,000 Sudanese immigrants are bracing for the possibility they’ll lose their humanitarian protections by Monday.

Oil and gas companies will now be permitted to kill polar bears and Pacific walruses off the northern coast of Alaska so long as such killings are “unintentional,” according to a new Trump administration rule.

The US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) on Friday finalized a rule change that would shield fossil fuel companies from legal liability if they engage in the “incidental, unintentional” killing of the animals “during year-round oil and gas industry activities in the Beaufort Sea… and adjacent northern coast of Alaska.”

Under the rule change, which is scheduled to last through 2031, the FWS “will issue letters of authorization” that sign off on the incidental killing of wildlife upon request by oil and gas companies.

“Over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite the industry that it had promised to its workers and to the public. Rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation,” says Tan, who was pushed out of Microsoft after raising objections to the company’s ties to fossil fuel companies.

Silicon Valley’s slide to the right was influenced by corporate backlash to labor’s demands, explains Redwine, who was fired from Kickstarter for union organizing. She says she hopes to inspire a new generation of tech workers to organize “within these tech oligarchs’ own empires, to stand up and push back.”

Israeli settlers conducting an assault on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank amid their autumn olive harvest also attacked a U.S. journalist on Friday, sending her to the hospital as she and other journalists were documenting the coordinated violent raid.

Heidi Levine, a veteran photojournalist for The Washington Post, was donning a “press” vest when settlers chased her and a group of other journalists away from the site of the raid on Palestinian families. They knocked her to the ground, stole her phone and cameras, and beat her.

“They just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times,” Levine said. Video of the attack shows Levine on the ground being beaten by masked assailants.

Abdul-Rahman al-Nashash, 11, holds onto the edge of a chair and pushes his left leg into a plastic prosthetic that doesn’t fit him anymore. The bone that was cut two years ago has kept growing inside, and it presses painfully against his skin.

His doctors told him to stop wearing it. He wears it anyway, every morning, pulling the straps tight and rolling his pants down so no one sees the plastic before he takes his first step. He bites his lip when it hurts and holds his shoulders straight so no one can tell he is limping.

“He forces himself to wear it,” his mother said, “just so no one knows he has a disability.”

Before the genocide, al-Nashash played for a local soccer club, and he would chase the ball across a dirt field until the sun went down. He is the eldest son in his family, and he was the one his mother leaned on at home. When she needed water, he was the one who ran to carry the heavy gallon of water, and he never got tired. Now, he is not able.

When he finally takes the prosthetic off, he sits curled up. He is waiting for his third surgery, and his mother said he will need one every year.

The report, published today by Environment America Research & Policy Center, found hotspots for the toxics, including the Mississippi River and Lake Ontario, and warns that this widespread pollution is likely “just the tip of the iceberg,” as it represents only a sampling of US waterways tested for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

“The report underscores what is really a much bigger problem than what most people realize,” said Tony Spaniola, co-chair of the Great Lakes PFAS Action Network. “If anything, the report dramatically understates the problem.”

The findings come as the Trump administration rolls back policies aimed at reducing PFAS in drinking water. Critics say such moves will only worsen people’s exposure to the chemicals, which are linked to some cancers, high cholesterol, decreased immune response to vaccines, liver damage, thyroid problems, reproductive issues and other health issues.

Health officials in Pennsylvania have announced another death related to measles, the sixth overall in the state and the U.S. since the beginning of this year.

Officials identified the person who died as a 39-year-old woman from Franklin County. The individual was reportedly not vaccinated against the virus. The county coroner described the cause of death as a “probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.”

The state is facing a large measles outbreak, accounting for about a quarter of all measles cases identified across the country since January 1, 2026. As of Tuesday morning, over 4,260 measles cases have been reported in the U.S., 1,152 of them from Pennsylvania alone. Both South Carolina and Texas are also reporting close to 1,000 measles cases.

Notably, the vast majority of people who have tested positive for measles are unvaccinated, with only 3 percent of cases affecting a person who has received the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) shot.

Among the deaths were two infants in Lancaster County, an area about 60 miles west of Philadelphia and the epicenter of the Pennsylvania outbreak. A newborn had congenital measles, which was passed in utero through an unvaccinated mother who was infected. It is not clear whether the other infant, who was reportedly 6 weeks old at the time of death and had a genetic birth disorder, was exposed in utero or after birth.

Some Pennsylvania-based doctors have experienced an uptick in anxious questions from patients about the implications of measles on just about all aspects of pregnancy care: What do more cases mean for a current pregnancy? On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas that the Indigenous Lucayan people called Guanahani. He continued on to Cuba and Hispaniola and, on later voyages, to other parts of the Caribbean, but he never set foot in what is now the continental United States. It makes little sense for a country to honor a man who never reached it, and even less to credit him with discovering a place that millions of people already called home. And it makes even less given what Columbus actually did in the places where he stepped foot: He rounded up Indigenous people in the Caribbean, chained them, and sent them as slaves to Spain. And when Indigenous communities rose up in resistance, he ordered his soldiers to “spread terror,” maiming and slaughtering civilians en masse using firearms, dogs, swords, and pikes.

But despite all this, in 1937, the United States established a federal holiday in his name anyway.

One of the most visible consequences of global warming is the increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, such as the powerful nor’easter that hammered the East Coast and mid-Atlantic for several days in late September with heavy rain, winds, and flooding. Indeed, a wide array of scientific studies over the past couple of decades have shown how human-caused climate change affects the intensity, frequency, and impact of extreme weather — from wildfires in the U.S. and Australia to record-setting flooding in China. And now, a major study prepared by two dozen scientists from across the globe has found a link between industrial emissions and the warming of the snow-capped Himalayan region that led to the collapse of the glacier that caused the catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet last month, in which over 1,300 people were killed while thousands are still missing.

title: I Carry the Key to My Destroyed Home in Gaza to Keep Alive My Dream of Returning
content:
The word “ceasefire” entered the news on October 11, 2025, but it has still not entered our lives as a reality.

On the night of March 18, 2025, while we were observing Ramadan, my family and I woke to the sound of very loud explosions, one after another.

We all woke up frightened and began asking my father, “What happened? Has the war returned?”

My father did not answer. No one knew anything.

We stayed together, waiting for morning, not knowing what was happening.

We had not expected the first ceasefire to be broken. We had already spent nearly a year living through war, and we had been looking forward to Ramadan with the hope that it would come without the bombing and fear.

The first ceasefire in Gaza had lasted nearly two months before Israel resumed its airstrikes that day, ending the period of relative calm that had begun on January 19, 2025.

Then everything became quiet. We ate suhoor, the early morning meal eaten before the daily fast of Ramadan begins, we prayed Fajr (the pre-dawn prayer), and went back to sleep.

But we were overwhelmed by grief and exhaustion. We loved Ramadan, and we had been waiting for it for a whole year, hoping that it would finally be a time to feel some happiness after a year of displacement, hunger, war, and exhaustion.

We are about to close out three years and enter another since Israel invaded Gaza, but we are not leaving the war behind to begin a new life. We are entering yet another year without knowing when this war will end — or whether it will end at all.

The fear remains. The destruction remains. The threats remain. It feels as though each passing year does not bring us closer to an end, but closer to the possibility of another war.

Despite everything we are living through in Gaza, we understand what it means to live one day at a time — to hold on to every simple moment we can still have. Imagine planning for another morning, perhaps for the simplest of things: going out with the friends you still have, or taking your family to the sea in the morning, amid all this destruction, simply to experience a moment that feels like life.

Then, as you are planning that ordinary morning, you hear a statement from Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, who said on September 22: “If even one Israeli soldier or civilian is abducted, the city of Gaza — with its homes and terrorist towers — will be evacuated southward of its one million residents.”

Each year, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which is primarily responsible for implementing the law, evaluates species and lists them as “endangered” or “threatened.” When federal activity or private development has the potential to harm a listed species or its habitat, project developers are required to consult with the Service or obtain a permit prior to construction.

When I left Gaza in 2024, after six months of living through genocide, I wanted one thing above all else: to spare my only child a life spent permanently at war. I did not want him to grow up believing that the whole world looked like Gaza.

But I left more than fifteen nieces and nephews behind. Many were still too young to understand the world they had been born into. They were learning what a home was, what a school was, what it meant to be alive, at the very moment those things were being destroyed around them.

I spent the next year and a half in Cairo. It took me a long time to learn how to inhabit ordinary life again. Whenever I saw a garden, a playground, a school, or children playing freely and safely in the street, I could not simply enjoy the sight. Gaza was always there, beneath it.

A garden brought back the rubble. A school brought back the children who no longer had one. Even safety became a reminder of those still denied it.

And she was still alive, marking what legal experts say is the first time a prisoner in the U.S. has survived one dose — let alone two — of lethal injection drugs.

Even if the outcome was unprecedented, what went wrong was not. Pike’s was the third Tennessee execution in 14 months to go awry. But as a reporter who has covered death row for nearly a decade and witnessed several executions, I know the state is not alone. The factors behind the breakdowns in Tennessee have popped up again and again across the country — and show how easily another botched execution could occur, even as soon as the ones planned Wednesday in Texas and next week in Florida.

title: Maryland Used Discredited Science to Convict a Woman of Murdering Her Newborn
content:

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Moira Akers was prosecuted and convicted of the murder of a newborn in 2022. She claims to have given birth to a stillborn baby in her home in Columbia, Maryland, in 2018.

Prosecutors doubted Akers’ story, using her online searches for abortion services and lack of prenatal care as evidence of ill intent. But it was a “forensic method” devised in the 17th century that proved key to Akers’ conviction.

The method, known as a “float test,” was designed to determine if a baby was stillborn or born alive by placing the lungs of a deceased fetus in water. If the lungs float, then they are aerated, meaning the baby was breathing and alive prior to their death.

In 2018, former Maryland chief medical examiner Dr. David Fowler signed the autopsy report that, using the float test as proof, determined that Akers’ baby died after Akers asphyxiated it. Fowler also testified in Akers’ trial. Prosecutors used Fowler’s testimony and autopsy report as evidence to convict Akers of second-degree murder in 2022.

I grew up walking the boardwalk in downtown Wilmington, North Carolina, peering into the froth of the Cape Fear River. The name came from 16th-century mariners who feared its mouth, which was known to churn ships into wrecks. But for the last few decades, there has been something new to fear in the river.

The Cape Fear River was tainted with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the Wilmington Star-News reported in 2017, a group of synthetic compounds now commonly known as “forever chemicals.”

As their name suggests, forever chemicals are renowned for their persistence. One of the strongest bonds in chemistry, carbon and fluorine, gives PFAS their nonstick properties. A seemingly endless list of products — dental floss, tampons, cellphones, wall paint, yoga pants, carpets, contact lenses, hair-straightening treatments, toilet paper — rely on those bonds to smooth, harden, slicken, and withstand heat and wear. “It is so much money,” Jacqueline Wheelock said to me about the monthly payment amount she will soon be forced to pay for her student loans.

Until last summer, she wasn’t thinking about this bill. Under the repayment plan known as SAVE (short for Saving on a Valuable Education), she could afford her payments, so she made them, month after month, never missing one or paying late. At the lowest, Wheelock paid $35 each month, and at the highest, she paid $110.

But now, in the wake of the Trump administration’s termination of SAVE, like 7 million other Americans, Wheelock must find a new plan — and soon — that works for her.

The problem is, she can’t find one that is remotely affordable. The cheapest plan available will cost her $285 but extend her repayment — and the total amount she pays — significantly. And the income-driven options that would qualify for the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) program, a program meant to relieve debtors after 10 years of qualifying payments and work in a public service job, would cost her between $693 and $733.

In an interview with NBC News’s Kristen Welker on the network’s “Meet the Press” program, Khanna was asked to respond to Sen. Tammy Duckworth’s (D-Illinois) suggestion last week that Democrats shift their focus from impeaching Trump.

“What I would encourage my colleagues to not do is…don’t be impeaching anybody. Let’s just get back to work, and maybe we can come back to compromises,” including restoring funding to parts of the government that the Trump administration drastically cut, Duckworth said.

Asked by Welker whether openly expressing a desire to impeach Trump a third time would be a mistake for Democrats, Khanna flatly rejected the premise.

“No, it’s not,” he said, “because [impeachment is] not about Donald Trump. He’s going to be a lame duck, and in my view, largely increasingly irrelevant.”

U.S. sources told NBC that a cruise missile hit the vessel the Marines were working on on September 14, leading to smoke inhalation and potential traumatic brain injuries, as some of them reported symptoms similar to those with concussions. They returned to duty soon after.

The vessel they were on was not a U.S. Navy ship, with officials only referring to it as a “maritime vessel.” The Marines “were operating as part of a battalion landing team during the Iranian anti-ship cruise missile attack,” NBC reported. The attack has not been publicly disclosed by the Department of Defense.

The report comes after the Pentagon’s latest update to the U.S.’s casualty list amid the war on Iran. Last week, the Pentagon quietly added 37 casualties to its public database. This included the eight Marines as well as 29 Navy sailors, bringing the total number of troops wounded during the war to 861.

Twenty-seven mathematicians who have received the most prestigious prize in mathematics — the Fields Medal — recently signed a declaration on artificial intelligence (AI) that highlights the disconnect between mathematicians and AI companies. The title of the statement — “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics” — gives the impression that it is about the AI tools themselves, but the text makes it clear that it is about the behavior of AI companies.

These companies are treating large open problems in mathematics as benchmarks to show off the capabilities of their tools. In doing so, they are rushing out results in a way that disempowers the mathematics community and ultimately impedes mathematical progress.

It is tempting to accept this as an inevitable outcome of more powerful AI tools. But doing this plays out in favor of the AI companies by allowing them to launder responsibility to the tools they build. AI companies would have you believe that the tools they are building are so powerful and so “intelligent” that they may set out to disempower and even destroy humanity of their own volition.

These Texas advocates call themselves “lionesses” for a reason: They say backing down is not in their nature.

In 2022, a small group of formerly incarcerated women formed the nonprofit Lioness Justice Impacted Women’s Alliance to empower communities to challenge harmful practices within the criminal legal system. Since that time, they have put a spotlight on what they argue are dangerous conditions caused by extreme heat and cold in Texas prisons.

Last week, Lioness, alongside two other organizations, won a major lawsuit against the Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) after a federal judge ruled that the state must air-condition all Texas prisons by the end of 2029. This change would fall in line with rules that already require Texas county jails to maintain temperatures between 65 and 85 degrees.

In a 150-page order, U.S. District Court Judge Robert Pitman noted that roughly 88,697 incarcerated people were housed in unairconditioned units heading into summer 2026, meaning TDCJ provides “cool beds” for only about 37 percent of its population.

title: Climate Crisis Made Rare East Coast Nor’easter Up to 50 Times More Likely
content:

A rare nor’easter storm system that ripped through the East Coast of the United States this weekend was made many times more likely to happen by the effects of the climate crisis.

As of Monday morning, the nor’easter was slowing down, with forecasters stating that the worst of the storm had passed. But reports of the storm’s impact on Sunday demonstrated its severity, with coastal flooding in some areas reaching the worst levels seen since Hurricane Sandy in 2012.

Heavy floods were reported on much of the East Coast, ranging from Delaware to New York. Several parts of New York City and Long Island were also reportedly hit hard by floods. In Surf City, New Jersey, wind speeds reached as high as 74 miles per hour. Waves in some parts of the coast reached as high as 20 feet.

At least one death has been counted as a result of the storm as of Sunday night: a 56-year-old New York City employee who was killed by a tree that fell during the storm. More than 130,000 people were also without power at some point.

title: Staying Grounded in the Face of Voter Intimidation
content:
Nonviolence trainers are teaching voters and volunteers how to manage fear and assess risk.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The ophthalmologist said he was going to touch my eyeball, then tilted my exam chair back in the darkness. I felt my body brace as movie torture scenes flashed through my mind. I noticed that I wasn’t breathing, so I practiced inhaling through my nose, and exhaling as steadily as I could for the rest of the exam.

Noticing our bodies and breathing intentionally may sound simple, but they are two of the practices that can keep us grounded when we are navigating scary or upsetting situations. As we approach a midterm election marred by threats of violence, I am practicing these skills as often as possible, not to suppress my feelings, but to be aware of how they are affecting me, so I can make conscious choices.

The forces of authoritarianism want us to feel knocked off center by the many ways they are trying to keep people from voting. Trump administration officials continue to suggest that ICE, FBI or other federal agents could be sent to polling places. It’s important that election volunteers and voters stay grounded to avoid playing into their hands. Two years after the water came, Jen and RJ Garbowicz still own a piece of St. Petersburg. It is an empty lot on a bayou off Tampa Bay, nearly an acre, with a few concrete pilings jutting out of the ground where their house once stood.

Hurricane Helene flooded it in September 2024. Hurricane Milton tore up the roof less than two weeks later. The couple had both flood and homeowners insurance. The flood policy paid in full, $250,000, and FEMA sent them about $33,000. Their homeowners insurer offered $2,279.41 against a $713,000 policy limit. They demolished what the hurricanes hadn’t and they estimate it will cost more than $1.5 million to rebuild their home.

Since then, the money has moved in strange directions. Their mortgage company is holding several hundred thousand dollars of the flood insurance payout until construction starts, which has been slowed as the couple wait on a permit. title: Missouri’s Abortion Rights Face a Second Vote in Two Years
content:
Abortion returns to ballots in Missouri and other states as voters and lawmakers reshape post-Roe policies.

After Missouri voters added abortion protections to the state constitution in 2024, Kelly McCoomb decided to keep her yard sign supporting the measure in the basement of her suburban St. Louis home.

Abortion access is important to McCoomb. She wants her daughter to grow up in a state where the option is available if needed, and the sign was a keepsake from the day Missourians voted to reverse the state’s near-total ban. McCoomb also couldn’t shake the feeling that she’d need to display the sign in her yard again soon.

“I have little faith in our Missouri government,” McCoomb said, sitting on her front porch.

Sure enough, just two years later, the state’s Republican-dominated legislature is asking Missouri voters to overturn the abortion protections they recently supported. The conflicting measures even have the same title: Amendment 3. But while a “yes” vote in 2024 supported adding protections to the state constitution, a “no” vote in 2026 would keep them. McCoomb covered the “YES” on her yard sign with a “NO” made from black duct tape before placing the sign back in her yard.

title: Supreme Court Shuts Down Missouri’s Gerrymandered Congressional Map
content:
After weeks of legal battles, Missouri voters will cast November ballots in the districts used in the past two elections.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Friday drove a stake through the heart of Missouri’s undead congressional map, ordering it be buried for the year and for voters to cast ballots in the districts they’ve used the past two election cycles.

In a unanimous decision, the court said that state law rules in the case.

“In short, as a matter of state law, the 2022 map — not the 2025 map — must be used in the 2026 congressional election,” states the ruling, which is unsigned.

The decision ends, for this election at least, Republicans’ effort to use a gerrymandered map to improve their chances of winning a seventh Missouri seat in the U.S. House.

It also caps three weeks of dramatic court action that changed the map in place for November five times, tested the jurisdiction and overlap of state and federal courts and exasperated local election officials responsible for conducting the vote.

Masafer Yatta is a 36-square-kilometer semi-desertic hilly area in the South Hebron region of the occupied West Bank. It directly overlooks the Naqab desert and extends west to the edge of the Dead Sea Valley. The hills are adjacent to the 1949 Armistice line, known today as the Green Line and viewed internationally as the borders of Israel proper. This strategic location makes it crucial for urban and agricultural growth south of the West Bank. For Israel, Masafer Yatta is treated as a buffer zone separating Israel proper from the deeper Palestinian demographic presence — a zone that needs to be emptied of Palestinians.

Emerging from the #Not1More campaign organized by undocumented activists and groups like Puente and Juntos in 2014, and gaining momentum with concerted organizing by grassroots groups such as Mijente, Detention Watch Network, Freedom for Immigrants, La Resistencia, and many others, the movement to abolish ICE has been building for years.

However, to have a mainstream organization such as Amnesty International — which has 7 million members and a global budget nearing $400 million, and which is often turned to by corporate media outlets — officially endorsing the explicit call for abolition signals a shift in the movement’s momentum as public support for ICE dwindles.

An estimate from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on the number of noncitizen residents registered to vote in Nevada has dropped from an initial claim of nearly 16,000, down to 185, and eventually to zero, just weeks after President Donald Trump cited the claim during a campaign rally in a push to purge several states’ voter rolls.

DHS officials initially informed Nevada election officials that they had reason to believe that 15,903 noncitizens were registered to vote in the Silver State. But last month, department officials acknowledged that number was overblown, while maintaining that 185 noncitizen residents could potentially vote.

Nevada investigated those names and found that none of them were noncitizens.

“As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” Nevada Deputy Attorney General Greg Ott wrote in a letter to DHS.

In a statement regarding the department’s claims, Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar called out DHS for its error, and for continuing to push similar false claims elsewhere.
